lessons.title: The Armistice and the Aims of the Peacemakers
lessons.description: How November 1918 ended the fighting and what Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George each wanted.
lessons.content_html:
A War That Ended Without an Invasion

By autumn 1918 Germany was exhausted. The Allied naval blockade had pushed civilians to near-starvation, the army was in retreat after the failed Spring Offensive, and revolution was breaking out in Kiel and Munich. On 9 November Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated, and two days later, in a railway carriage at Compiègne, German representatives signed an armistice that took effect at 11am on 11 November 1918. Crucially, no Allied soldier had set foot on German soil. This shaped everything that followed: many Germans believed they had not really been beaten on the battlefield, while the French were determined that this time Germany must be made to pay.

Key Fact

The Paris Peace Conference opened in January 1919. The dominant figures — the Big Three — were Woodrow Wilson (USA), Georges Clemenceau (France) and David Lloyd George (Britain). Italy’s Vittorio Orlando attended but had less influence.

Woodrow Wilson and the Fourteen Points

The American president had set out his peace aims a full ten months before the armistice. In a speech to Congress on 8 January 1918 he proposed the Fourteen Points. The points called for open treaties (no more secret diplomacy), free trade, freedom of the seas, disarmament, the adjustment of colonial claims to consider local populations, and the principle of national self-determination for the peoples of Europe. The fourteenth and most ambitious point called for a general association of nations — what would become the League of Nations — to guarantee the independence of every state.

Wilson’s thinking was idealistic. The United States had joined the war late, in April 1917, and had suffered far fewer casualties than the European powers. Wilson believed a fair peace was the only route to a lasting peace; a vengeful settlement would only sow the seeds of another war. He arrived in Europe to enormous public welcomes, presenting himself as a statesman above the petty hatreds of the Old World.

Georges Clemenceau and French Security

France had been invaded by Germany twice in fifty years — in 1870 and again in 1914. The fighting on the Western Front had taken place largely on French soil. Around 1.4 million French soldiers were dead and northern France lay devastated, its mines flooded and its factories destroyed. Clemenceau, nicknamed ‘the Tiger’, had no interest in idealism. His priority was simple: France must never face another German invasion.

That meant making Germany pay for reconstruction through heavy reparations, taking back Alsace-Lorraine (lost to Germany in 1871), demilitarising the Rhineland to create a buffer zone, and stripping Germany of its army, navy and air force. Some French generals, including Marshal Foch, wanted to push the German border back to the Rhine. Clemenceau pushed for the harshest terms the British and Americans would accept.

The British prime minister had just won the December 1918 ‘Khaki Election’ on slogans like ‘Hang the Kaiser’ and ‘Make Germany Pay’. British public opinion wanted vengeance. Privately, however, Lloyd George worried about the long term. He did not want Germany to be so weakened that the Soviet revolutionary movement spread westward into central Europe, and he recognised that a recovered Germany was an essential trading partner. He also wanted to protect Britain’s naval supremacy and its empire — including taking former German colonies as mandates.

Lloyd George therefore played a middleman’s role — tougher than Wilson on reparations, softer than Clemenceau on Germany’s long-term position. His chief contribution was to push reparations to a punishing but ambiguous figure while keeping Germany intact as a state.

Conflicting Aims, Inevitable Compromise

The three leaders met in Paris from January 1919, often in private ‘Council of Four’ sessions with Orlando. Their disagreements were sharp. Wilson wanted lenient terms; Clemenceau wanted Germany dismembered; Lloyd George wanted a workable Germany that could pay reparations and trade. A common claim by some students is that Versailles was uniquely punitive, but it is worth remembering that the terms Germany itself had imposed on Russia at Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 stripped Russia of one third of its population and most of its industry — far harsher than anything Germany would receive.

Wilson got his League of Nations and a redrawn map based largely on self-determination — but only four of his Fourteen Points were fully accepted, and the US Senate would later refuse to ratify the treaty at all. Clemenceau secured Alsace-Lorraine, a demilitarised Rhineland and large reparations — but not the permanent French occupation of the Rhine he had wanted. Lloyd George took German colonies and weakened the German navy — but the harshness of the final terms troubled him; he reportedly remarked that they would have to fight Germany again within twenty years.

Key Fact

Each peacemaker arrived with different priorities: Wilson wanted a fair peace and a League of Nations; Clemenceau wanted French security through a weakened Germany; Lloyd George wanted to punish Germany without crippling it as a future trading partner. The Treaty of Versailles was the compromise between these aims.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on peacemaking, the examiner is looking for causal links between events, not a list of dates. Each event you describe should connect to the next: the armistice halted fighting because Germany faced collapse, which forced the peacemakers to meet, which exposed the differences in aims that shaped the treaty. Practise writing in three or four linked steps with phrases like ‘this triggered’, ‘as a result’, ‘which meant that’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The November 1918 armistice ended the fighting without an Allied invasion of Germany — a fact that shaped both German resentment and Allied determination to dictate terms.
  • The Big Three brought sharply different aims to Paris: Wilson’s idealism, Clemenceau’s demand for security, Lloyd George’s search for a balanced peace.
  • Versailles would be a compromise — pleasing none of the peacemakers fully, and storing up problems that would shape the next twenty years.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a speech by David Lloyd George to the British House of Commons, March 1919, during the Paris Peace Conference.
‘We must take care that the peace we make is not so harsh that it will breed another war within a generation. Germany must be punished, but a Germany driven to despair will be a Germany of revolution and rearmament. The dragon’s teeth, once sown, will spring up again.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Lloyd George gives for moderating the peace terms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• A harsh peace risks another war within a generation (‘breed another war’).
• A Germany driven to despair will turn to revolution.
• A despairing Germany will rearm.
• The metaphor of ‘dragon’s teeth’ implies that vengeful terms produce future enemies.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Germany moved from military strength in spring 1918 to signing the armistice in November 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Spring Offensive, Hundred Days, blockade, naval mutiny, abdication, Compiègne); reaches the armistice through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• March 1918: Ludendorff Spring Offensive made huge initial gains but exhausted German troops.
• August 1918: Allied counter-attack (the Hundred Days) drove Germany back beyond the Hindenburg Line.
• The naval blockade caused civilian starvation, undermining home-front morale.
• October 1918: German High Seas Fleet mutiny at Kiel sparked wider revolution.
• 9 November 1918: Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated; new republican government sought peace.
• 11 November 1918: Armistice signed at Compiègne, ending the fighting at 11am.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter sent by Georges Clemenceau to a French general in February 1919, drawn from the records of the French Foreign Ministry.
‘Twice in my lifetime I have seen our cities burned and our farms ruined by German armies. I will not sign a treaty that does not place Germany under restraint for a generation. The Americans speak of fairness; the British of trade. I speak of survival.’

Source C: An extract from an article by Wickham Steed, editor of The Times newspaper in London, published in May 1919.
‘President Wilson came to Paris with the goodwill of all Europe. He has, however, allowed his Fourteen Points to be filed down one by one to satisfy French anxieties and British electoral promises. The treaty that emerges is a compromise that fully reflects no single vision.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the aims of the peacemakers in 1919. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Clemenceau frames French aims as survival, dismissing American idealism and British trade focus. Provenance: a private letter from the leading French negotiator to a general; likely to express genuine views without diplomatic varnish. Own knowledge: France had lost roughly 1.4 million soldiers; Alsace-Lorraine and the Rhineland buffer were direct expressions of this thinking.
Source C — Content: argues Wilson’s Fourteen Points were diluted to suit French and British concerns. Provenance: a major British newspaper editor in May 1919, well-informed but writing for a public audience and reflecting British liberal opinion. Own knowledge: only four of the Fourteen Points were accepted in full; the Senate would reject the treaty in 1920.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding French priorities but partial; C is useful as informed contemporary commentary but reflects one British viewpoint.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a memo by Woodrow Wilson to his close adviser Edward House, written aboard the USS George Washington in December 1918, drawn from the Wilson Papers held at the US Library of Congress.
‘Tell our delegation that we go to Paris not as conquerors but as conciliators. The peoples of Europe expect a new order built on justice. If we permit the old diplomacy of secret bargains and territorial revenge to prevail, we shall have fought in vain.’

Source E: An extract from a 1919 cartoon caption in the British satirical magazine Punch, showing Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George round a small table marked ‘Peace’.
‘Three doctors with three different prescriptions for the same patient. The pity is that the patient is Europe.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The disagreements between the Big Three were the main reason the Treaty of Versailles failed to satisfy any of them.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows Wilson’s idealistic agenda; Source E captures the gap between the three leaders pictorially.
• Wilson’s Fourteen Points were repeatedly compromised; Clemenceau did not get a permanent French occupation of the Rhineland; Lloyd George worried Versailles would lead to another war.
Challenging the claim:
• Other factors mattered: domestic politics (the British ‘Khaki Election’, US Senate hostility to entanglement); the absence of Germany and Russia from the conference; the genuine difficulty of reconciling self-determination with multi-ethnic borders.
• Some compromises were not signs of failure but of negotiation working as intended.
Judgement: differences in aims were a major factor, but compounded by domestic constraints and the practical limits of redrawing Europe.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British civil servant Maurice Hankey, secretary to the British Cabinet, recording a conversation with Lloyd George on 30 March 1919.
‘The PM said the French were impossible — they wanted to destroy Germany altogether and would not listen to reason. Wilson, he said, was clever but tired and increasingly stubborn. The PM’s own task, he believed, was to hold the centre and prevent the peace from being either too soft or too vengeful.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying Lloyd George’s role at the Paris Peace Conference.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: Source F reveals Lloyd George’s view of his own role as ‘holding the centre’ — useful evidence that he saw himself as a mediator between Wilson and Clemenceau.
• Provenance: It is a contemporaneous diary entry by his cabinet secretary, recording a private conversation — likely to capture genuine views.
• Own knowledge: This matches the historical record — Lloyd George pushed Clemenceau to moderate territorial demands and Wilson to accept reparations.
• Limitation worth noting: Hankey was a sympathetic insider, so the diary may flatter Lloyd George’s self-image.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the diplomatic steps from Wilson’s Fourteen Points speech in January 1918 to the opening of the Paris Peace Conference in January 1919.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the conference opening through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1918: Wilson set out the Fourteen Points to US Congress, providing a framework for peace.
• Spring/summer 1918: the Fourteen Points circulated widely, raising expectations across Europe.
• October 1918: Germany approached Wilson seeking armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points.
• November 1918: armistice signed; the Allied powers agreed in principle to use the Fourteen Points as a basis but with reservations on freedom of the seas and reparations.
• December 1918: Lloyd George won the ‘Khaki Election’ on harsh-peace slogans, narrowing his negotiating room.
• January 1919: the Paris Peace Conference opened, bringing Wilson’s ideals into direct collision with French and British priorities.

lessons.title: The Versailles Settlement: Terms and Diktat
lessons.description: The Treaty of Versailles in five blocks: territory, military, war guilt, reparations and the League.
lessons.content_html:
A Treaty Built in Five Blocks

The Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles on 28 June 1919 — deliberately the same room in which the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871. The German delegation was not invited to negotiate. They were handed the terms and told to sign or face renewed war. Germans called it the Diktat. The treaty had hundreds of clauses, but for revision it helps to think in five blocks: blame, money, military, territory and the League covenant.

Key Fact

The Treaty of Versailles, signed 28 June 1919, was structured around five themes: war guilt (blame), reparations (money), military restrictions, territorial changes, and the League of Nations covenant. Germany was forced to accept all five without negotiation.

Article 231: The War Guilt Clause

The war guilt clause was the legal foundation of the whole settlement. Article 231 declared that Germany and her allies were responsible for ‘all the loss and damage’ suffered by the Allies. This was not just an insult: it was the legal basis on which reparations could be demanded. Without an admission of guilt, Germany could not be billed.

For Germans this was the most hated clause. Most believed responsibility for the war was shared across Europe — that Germany had simply been defending itself after Russia mobilised. Branding their entire nation as the sole cause of years of slaughter felt like a public humiliation, and the war guilt clause poisoned political debate in Germany for the next twenty years.

Reparations

The exact figure was not fixed at Versailles itself. A Reparations Commission set the bill in 1921 at £6.6 billion (132 billion gold marks), to be paid in cash, coal, steel, ships and machinery over decades. The aim was both to compensate France and Belgium for war damage and to keep Germany economically weak.

The economist John Maynard Keynes, a British Treasury official at Paris, resigned in protest and published The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919), arguing reparations were so heavy they would wreck the German economy — and through trade, the European economy too. His warnings would seem prophetic when Germany’s 1923 hyperinflation arrived.

The treaty stripped Germany of the means to threaten its neighbours. The army was capped at 100,000 men — volunteers only, no conscription. Germany was banned from possessing tanks, submarines, military aircraft or heavy artillery. The navy was reduced to six battleships. The Rhineland — the strip of German territory along the French border — was permanently demilitarised, with no German troops or fortifications allowed within 50km of the Rhine.

For comparison, France kept an army of around 700,000 men. The intent was clear: Germany was to be a military pygmy beside her neighbours. From a French security perspective, this was the central achievement of the treaty.

Territorial Changes

Germany lost about 13% of its European territory and 12% of its population. In the west, Alsace-Lorraine returned to France after 48 years of German rule. The small districts of Eupen and Malmédy went to Belgium. North Schleswig was given to Denmark after a plebiscite. In the east, Germany lost Posen and West Prussia to recreated Poland, the latter forming the ‘Polish Corridor’. The port of Danzig (today’s Gdansk) became a Free City under League of Nations administration, giving Poland sea access without giving Poland the German-speaking city itself.

The Saar coalfield was placed under League administration for fifteen years, with its coal output going to France as compensation for damaged French mines. All of Germany’s overseas colonies — in Africa, the Pacific and China — were stripped away and redistributed to Britain, France, Belgium, Japan and South Africa as League of Nations mandates. Union with Austria (Anschluss) was specifically forbidden.

The first 26 articles of the treaty established the League of Nations. Germany was excluded from membership in 1919, treated as an outlaw state until it had ‘proved’ itself. Russia, ravaged by civil war and ideologically opposed, was also kept out. This meant the body intended to safeguard the new order began life without two of Europe’s largest powers, and (after the US Senate’s rejection in 1920) without the country whose president had designed it.

Was Versailles Uniquely Punitive?

Many Germans called Versailles a ‘Schmachfrieden’ — a peace of shame. To evaluate this fairly, compare it with the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk that Germany imposed on Russia in March 1918. Brest-Litovsk took a third of Russia’s population, a third of its agricultural land, and most of its iron and coal — territorial losses far greater than anything Germany faced. The Versailles peacemakers knew this; it shaped their willingness to dismiss German complaints about ‘harshness’. Versailles was harsh, but the claim that it was uniquely punitive ignores how Germany itself had behaved when it had won.

Key Fact

Reparations were set at £6.6 billion in 1921. The army was capped at 100,000 men. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Corridor and all overseas colonies. The Rhineland was demilitarised. Germany was excluded from the League of Nations.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Source Analysis, identify two distinct points from the source — do not paraphrase the same idea twice. Embed a very short quotation (three to five words) for each point. Do not waste time on provenance for the 4-marker; that is what the 12-mark Source Evaluation tests. Two clear points, briefly supported, is the formula.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Versailles imposed five blocks of terms: war guilt (Article 231), reparations (£6.6 billion in 1921), military restrictions (army capped at 100,000), territorial losses (13% of land), and the League covenant.
  • The treaty was a Diktat — Germany was excluded from negotiations and forced to sign on threat of renewed war.
  • Although harsh, Versailles was less severe than the terms Germany itself had imposed on Russia at Brest-Litovsk a year earlier.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the official text of the Treaty of Versailles, Article 231, signed 28 June 1919.
‘The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons why this clause was so resented in Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief supporting quotations.
Secure: Two clear reasons, briefly supported.
Developing: One clear point; second weak or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• It forced Germany alone to accept responsibility for the war (‘the responsibility of Germany’).
• It blamed the war on Germany’s ‘aggression’, which most Germans rejected.
• It implied Germany must pay for ‘all the loss and damage’ — opening the door to vast reparations.
• The clause spoke for ‘nationals’ as well as governments, suggesting Germany owed compensation to private citizens too.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the steps by which the Treaty of Versailles was finalised, from the opening of the Paris Peace Conference in January 1919 to its signing on 28 June 1919.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1919: Paris Peace Conference opened; the Council of Ten and later Council of Four met in private.
• March–April 1919: the Big Three argued bitterly over reparations and the Rhineland; Wilson briefly fell ill.
• 7 May 1919: terms presented to the German delegation at Versailles; Germany given 15 days to respond, later extended.
• Late May 1919: German counter-proposals were almost entirely rejected.
• 16 June 1919: an ultimatum demanded German signature within seven days or fighting would resume.
• 28 June 1919: the Treaty of Versailles signed in the Hall of Mirrors, five years to the day after the Sarajevo assassination.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a German government memorandum to the Allied powers, drafted by Foreign Minister Count Brockdorff-Rantzau in May 1919, drawn from German Foreign Office archives.
‘Such a peace would condemn the German people to perpetual slavery. The army restrictions leave us defenceless before any neighbour. The reparations cannot be met without ruining our economy. The territorial losses sever millions of Germans from the Reich. We cannot accept that one nation alone be branded as the cause of the war.’

Source C: An extract from a private letter by Marshal Ferdinand Foch, French commander-in-chief of Allied forces, to a colleague in June 1919, drawn from the Foch Papers held at the Service Historique de la Défense, Paris.
‘This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years. The Rhine is not the frontier; therefore Germany will rise again, and we shall be invaded a third time.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying reactions to the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Lists the four pillars of German objection: military, financial, territorial, war guilt. Provenance: official German government document by the leading negotiator; designed to put the German case to the Allies and to a domestic audience. Own knowledge: Germans called the treaty a Diktat; Article 231 became the most hated clause; reparations were eventually set at £6.6 billion.
Source C — Content: A French general dismisses the treaty as merely a 20-year armistice because the Rhine is not the western frontier. Provenance: a private letter by France’s most senior soldier; expresses unguarded views to a peer. Own knowledge: Foch had wanted the Rhine as the French frontier; Clemenceau accepted demilitarisation instead. Foch’s prediction proved accurate when Germany invaded France in 1940.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the German political reaction but partial as it omits the harsher Brest-Litovsk precedent; C is useful as informed French military opinion but reflects a particular hawkish position.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from John Maynard Keynes, ‘The Economic Consequences of the Peace’, published in London in late 1919. Keynes resigned from the British Treasury delegation at Paris in protest at the reparations terms.
‘The Treaty includes no provisions for the economic rehabilitation of Europe — nothing to make the defeated Central Empires into good neighbours, nothing to stabilise the new states of Europe, nothing to reclaim Russia. The reparations clauses are dictated by passion rather than sense.’

Source E: An extract from a 1919 editorial in the French newspaper Le Figaro, the day after the treaty was signed.
‘At last, justice. Germany has been made to pay for what she did. The Rhineland is empty of her troops, her army is broken, her colonies are gone. France can sleep safe behind these guarantees.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The Treaty of Versailles was an economic disaster waiting to happen.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument using both sources; judgement supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources; provenance or knowledge limited; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D: the warnings of an informed insider that the economic terms ignored European recovery.
• Reparations of £6.6 billion (1921) outpaced Germany’s capacity to pay; the 1923 hyperinflation followed German default and the French occupation of the Ruhr.
• Loss of the Saar coalfield, the merchant fleet, and all colonies stripped Germany of significant wealth.
Challenging the claim:
• Source E: French opinion saw the treaty as security, not economic ruin.
• Germany only paid a fraction of the reparations bill; the treaty was repeatedly renegotiated (Dawes 1924, Young 1929).
• Other factors caused Germany’s collapse — the 1929 Wall Street Crash and Depression were the decisive blow, not Versailles itself.
Judgement: the economic terms were severe and short-sighted, but the claim of inevitable disaster underestimates the role of later shocks.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British civil servant Sir Eric Phipps, who was attached to the British Embassy in Paris in 1919. Diary entry for 7 May 1919.
‘Today the German delegation was handed the treaty. They were not permitted to debate it. Brockdorff-Rantzau read his reply seated, which was taken as an insult. The whole proceeding had the air of a sentencing rather than a negotiation.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying how the Treaty of Versailles was presented to Germany.

lessons.title: Reactions to the Treaty and the Wider Settlement
lessons.description: Allied disagreements, German fury, and the strengths and weaknesses of the wider 1919-20 settlement.
lessons.content_html:
Three Audiences, Three Reactions

When the Treaty of Versailles was signed in June 1919, three groups had to live with the result: the Allied powers themselves, defeated Germany, and the patchwork of new states drawn out of the collapsed Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires. Each was disappointed, although for very different reasons. The four other peace treaties of 1919-1920 — Saint-Germain with Austria, Trianon with Hungary, Neuilly with Bulgaria and Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire — together formed the wider settlement that redrew the political map of Europe.

Key Fact

Versailles was only one of five treaties: Saint-Germain (1919, Austria), Trianon (1920, Hungary), Neuilly (1919, Bulgaria) and Sèvres (1920, Ottoman Empire). Together they dismantled four empires and created or recognised states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Austria.

Allied Reactions

Each of the victorious powers found something to dislike. In the United States, the Senate, controlled by Republicans hostile to international entanglement, twice refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, in November 1919 and March 1920. The USA never joined the League of Nations — depriving Wilson’s creation of the country whose president had designed it. Italy felt cheated. Pre-war British and French promises (the secret 1915 Treaty of London) had drawn Italy into the war with offers of Adriatic territory. At Paris, Italy was denied parts of the Dalmatian coast and the city of Fiume, leading to nationalist outrage and the slogan ‘mutilated victory’.

France felt the treaty had not gone far enough. Marshal Foch wanted the Rhine as the western frontier and feared Germany would simply rebuild. Britain, by contrast, was already worrying that the terms were too harsh; Lloyd George privately predicted another war within a generation. Japan, the only non-European great power at Paris, was offended when Wilson rejected its proposed clause on racial equality, although it gained former German Pacific islands as mandates.

German Objections

For Germany, the treaty was a national humiliation. The most explosive idea to emerge was the ‘stab-in-the-back myth’ (Dolchstosslegende). Promoted by right-wing politicians and former generals, it claimed that the German army had not been defeated in the field; it had been betrayed by socialists, communists and Jews on the home front. The civilian politicians who signed the armistice and the treaty — the ‘November Criminals’ — were branded traitors. This narrative would poison the new Weimar Republic from its birth and provide ready material for Hitler’s rise.

Specific objections were sharp. Article 231 was rejected as morally false. Reparations were rejected as unpayable. The army cap left Germany unable to defend its borders. Territorial losses cut roughly six million Germans off into other countries — in violation, Germans argued, of Wilson’s own principle of self-determination. The ban on Anschluss with Austria struck many as proof that self-determination was applied selectively.

The peacemakers tried to apply self-determination to central Europe but found it impossible to draw clean ethnic borders. Czechoslovakia contained roughly three million Germans in the Sudetenland, plus Slovaks, Hungarians, Poles and Ruthenians. Yugoslavia bound together Serbs, Croats and Slovenes — communities with different religions, scripts and recent histories. Poland was reborn after 123 years and immediately faced disputes with Germany, Russia, Lithuania and Ukraine.

These successor states were small, surrounded by larger neighbours, and contained sizeable ethnic minorities who often resented being citizens of the wrong country. Treaties tried to protect minority rights through the League, but enforcement was weak. Hungary, which had lost two-thirds of its pre-war territory under Trianon, became the most revisionist state in Europe — and the disputed Sudetenland would later become Hitler’s lever for cracking the post-war order.

Strengths of the Settlement

It is easy to dwell on the failures, but the settlement also had genuine strengths. It produced a stable peace in Europe for over a decade. It applied self-determination to Poland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Finland after generations of imperial rule. It dismantled four authoritarian empires and replaced them with mostly democratic governments. It created the League of Nations — for all its later weaknesses, the first international organisation devoted to preventing war. The 1925 Locarno treaties and Germany’s admission to the League in 1926 suggested the system could evolve.

The settlement was undermined from the start by three structural problems. First, the United States, the strongest power, walked away. Second, Russia, ravaged by civil war and ideologically opposed, was excluded. Third, Germany was treated as a defeated outlaw rather than a future partner. The League was therefore born without three of the world’s most important countries. The settlement also relied on small new states defending themselves against future German or Russian recovery — an unrealistic burden, as 1939 would prove.

Key Fact

The wider settlement’s greatest strength was applying self-determination to many peoples for the first time. Its greatest weakness was the absence of the USA, the exclusion of Russia, and the alienation of Germany. The League of Nations was therefore born missing three of the world’s most important powers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Source Evaluation, you must integrate three things: source content (what does it say?), provenance (who wrote it, when, why?), and your own contextual knowledge (what do you know that confirms or qualifies the source?). Top-band answers do all three for both sources and reach a substantiated overall judgement on usefulness. Answers that handle only two of the three elements are capped below the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reactions to the settlement varied: the USA refused to join the League, Italy spoke of ‘mutilated victory’, France thought the terms too soft, and Germany rejected the treaty as a Diktat.
  • In Germany, the stab-in-the-back myth and the ‘November Criminals’ label discredited Weimar politicians and provided fuel for later extremism.
  • The settlement applied self-determination broadly but created small successor states with ethnic minorities, Russian and German neighbours, and limited capacity to defend themselves — weaknesses Hitler would exploit.

Source B: An extract from a German newspaper editorial in the Berliner Tageblatt, published 29 June 1919, the day after the signing of the Treaty of Versailles.
‘Today we have signed under duress what we will never accept in our hearts. The treaty leaves Germany neither a great power nor a free nation. The war guilt clause is a public lie. The reparations are slavery. We did not lose this war on the battlefield; we were betrayed at home.’

Source C: An extract from a private memorandum by British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour, December 1919, recently released from the Foreign Office archives.
‘The settlement is imperfect, but it is a settlement. The Germans complain because they cannot do otherwise. Our task now is to bind them by gradual concessions into the new order. The League will be the chief instrument of this work.’

Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a public German rejection of all four pillars of the treaty, including the stab-in-the-back claim. Provenance: a German newspaper the day after signing, reflecting public mood and shaping it. Own knowledge: this matches the wider German rhetoric of ‘November Criminals’ and Diktat; the stab-in-the-back myth was a powerful but historically false narrative.
Source C — Content: a measured British view that gradual concessions will integrate Germany. Provenance: a private memorandum by the British Foreign Secretary, written for an internal audience and so likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: matches Lloyd George’s view that Germany must be a partner; foreshadows the Dawes Plan, Locarno and Germany’s 1926 League entry.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German public reaction but partial — it amplifies the stab-in-the-back myth; C is useful for moderate British policy thinking but reflects only one strand of British opinion.

Source D: An extract from a 1920 speech by Tomáš Masaryk, first President of Czechoslovakia, delivered at the Old Town Square in Prague.
‘We are a young state surrounded by larger neighbours, with a German minority within our borders and Hungarians and Poles disputing our edges. We must learn quickly to be both democratic and strong, or we shall not survive. The League of Nations is our shield, but we must also be our own.’

Source E: An extract from a 1920 letter by Hungarian politician Albert Apponyi to a Hungarian magazine, after the signing of the Treaty of Trianon.
‘Hungary has been broken into pieces. Three million of our countrymen now live under foreign rule. The principle of self-determination has been applied against us, never for us. There can be no peace in this region until our injuries are repaired.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The wider peace settlement of 1919-1920 created more problems than it solved.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.

Mastering: Sustained argument engaging the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear argument using both sources; judgement supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources; provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows the fragility of new states with ethnic minorities and powerful neighbours.
• Source E reflects Hungarian revisionism after Trianon — territory and population losses that left the country revisionist.
• The settlement excluded the USA, alienated Germany, isolated Russia, and left small successor states unable to defend themselves; this collapsed in the 1930s.
Challenging the claim:
• Self-determination was applied to Poland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Finland for the first time in centuries.
• The settlement produced over a decade of relative peace; the Locarno treaties and German League entry suggested it could evolve.
• Some problems were inherited from the war itself, not created by the treaties.
Judgement: the settlement contained genuine reforms but its structural exclusions and minority issues outweighed its successes in the long run.

lessons.title: The League of Nations: Structure and Membership
lessons.description: How the League was formed, organised, and which great powers joined or stayed out.
lessons.content_html:
A New Idea: Collective Security

When Wilson’s Fourteen Points called for a ‘general association of nations’, he was proposing something the world had never tried. The idea, set out in the League’s founding document — the Covenant — was collective security: aggression against any member would be treated as aggression against all, deterring war by threatening combined response. The Covenant formed the first 26 articles of the Treaty of Versailles. It came into force on 10 January 1920, the day the treaty took effect, and the League’s headquarters opened in Geneva.

Key Fact

The League of Nations opened in Geneva on 10 January 1920. Its founding document was the Covenant. Its core principle was collective security — that an attack on one member would be met by all.

The Bodies of the League

The League had four main parts. The Council was a small executive body for handling disputes. It originally had four permanent members — Britain, France, Italy and Japan — and four (later more) non-permanent members elected by the Assembly. The Council met three times a year and in emergency sessions. The Assembly was the parliament of the League, with all member states represented. Each state had one vote, regardless of size. The Assembly met annually and dealt with budgets, admitting new members and broad policy.

A common student error is to confuse the two: think of the Council as the engine room and the Assembly as the debating chamber. Both, fatally, required unanimity for major decisions, meaning a single member could veto action. Behind these political bodies sat the Secretariat (the civil service, headed by a Secretary-General) and the Permanent Court of International Justice (the legal arm, based in The Hague).

Beyond political dispute resolution, the League ran a network of specialist agencies that did real work for ordinary people. The International Labour Organization (ILO) lobbied for shorter hours, fairer pay and bans on child labour. The Health Committee tackled cholera, malaria and leprosy and laid foundations for what became the World Health Organization. The High Commission for Refugees, led from 1921 by Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, helped resettle hundreds of thousands of people displaced by the war and the Russian Civil War. The League’s Slavery Commission worked to end the slave trade in Africa, and Mandate Commissions monitored the territories taken from Germany and the Ottomans. These agencies were among the League’s most lasting successes — they outlived the League itself, becoming the basis of much of the modern UN system.

The Powers of the League

When a member broke the rules, the League had three escalating responses. First came moral condemnation — a public statement that the aggressor was in the wrong. Second, economic sanctions — cutting off trade or finance. Third, in theory, military force — member states would contribute troops to enforce League decisions. In practice, the third option was almost never used because the League had no army of its own and members had no obligation to send troops.

This made the League essentially a discussion forum backed by economic threat. Where great powers were the aggressors and willing to bear sanctions, there was little the League could do.

Membership: A League of Missing Powers

The League launched with 42 members in 1920. By the late 1920s membership rose past 50, and by 1934 it reached 58. But the membership story is largely a story of missing or temporary great powers.

The United States, despite Wilson’s leading role in designing the League, never joined — the Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles in 1919-20. The Soviet Union was excluded as ideologically hostile after the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution; it would not join until 1934, only to be expelled in 1939 for invading Finland. Germany was excluded as a defeated outlaw and only joined in 1926, after the rehabilitation of Locarno and Stresemann’s reconciliation diplomacy. In 1933, the year Hitler came to power, Germany resigned from the League; Japan resigned the same year over the Manchurian crisis. Italy left in 1937 after invading Abyssinia. By 1939 the League’s great-power membership was effectively just Britain and France.

Key Fact

The USA never joined the League. Germany joined 1926, left 1933. Japan founding member, left 1933. The USSR joined 1934, expelled 1939. By 1939 the only remaining great-power members were Britain and France.

Eric Drummond and the Civil Service

The League’s first Secretary-General, the British diplomat Eric Drummond, served from 1920 to 1933. He built the Secretariat into a genuinely international civil service, recruiting staff loyal to the League rather than their home states. This was a quiet but important innovation: it created the model for the UN civil service that followed in 1945. Drummond’s low-key style worked well in the 1920s when the League was fighting for legitimacy, but the system would prove no match for great-power aggression in the 1930s.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Source Analysis question on the League’s structure or membership, look for two specific facts in the source rather than a general impression. Examiners want particular powers, dates or mechanisms named. A common mistake is to write ‘the League was weak’ without specifying why — identify the unanimity rule, missing great powers, or the absence of a League army.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The League opened in Geneva in January 1920 with the Covenant as its rulebook and collective security as its principle.
  • Its main bodies were the Council (small executive), Assembly (all members, one vote each), Secretariat (civil service) and Permanent Court — with specialist agencies on labour, health and refugees.
  • The League’s critical weakness was missing or temporary great powers: the USA never joined, Germany only from 1926, the USSR only from 1934 — and by 1939 only Britain and France remained.

‘The League’s headquarters at Geneva is busy and serious — but it is a European body. Without American membership, decisions taken here have no weight in Washington and little weight in the wider world. The League may yet prove its worth, but the absence of the largest economy on earth is a permanent shadow.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the early difficulties faced by the League of Nations. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: identifies US absence as the chief difficulty; describes the League acting as ‘a body of friends rather than a body of judges’. Provenance: a private letter from the Secretary-General to a peer; likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: matches the wider record — the US Senate’s 1919-20 rejection deprived the League of its strongest power.
Source C — Content: stresses the absence of American economic power. Provenance: an American newspaper, reporting back to a US audience; reflects American liberal pro-League opinion. Own knowledge: confirms US economic dominance — by the 1920s the USA was the world’s largest economy; without it sanctions had limited bite.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the official insider view but partial; C is useful as informed contemporary commentary but reflects pro-League American opinion.

‘In the past year the International Labour Organization has secured 17 conventions on hours of work and protection of women and children in industry. The Health Committee has assisted in containing typhus epidemics in eastern Europe. The High Commission for Refugees has issued more than 200,000 Nansen passports to stateless persons.’

Source E: An extract from a 1926 speech in the British House of Commons by Stanley Baldwin, Conservative Prime Minister.
‘The League has done valuable humanitarian work, but its political achievements are slighter. Where two small nations dispute, the League can settle the matter. Where a great power is the offender, the League is silent. The Council’s unanimity rule guarantees this.’

Secure: Clear argument using both sources; judgement supported.
Developing: Some argument; reference to both sources; provenance or own knowledge limited.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D: the agencies achieved real humanitarian results — ILO conventions, Nansen passports, public health.
• 1920s political successes: Aaland Islands, Upper Silesia, Bulgaria.
• German League entry in 1926 suggested the system was integrating former enemies.
Challenging the claim:
• Source E: the unanimity rule and great-power exemption were structural problems already visible by 1926.
• Vilna and Corfu showed great powers ignored the League.
• The USA never joined; the USSR was excluded; the League covered Europe more effectively than the wider world.
Judgement: in the 1920s the League was effective in humanitarian work and small disputes; ineffective whenever a great power was the aggressor.

Source F: An extract from a 1926 speech by Gustav Stresemann, German Foreign Minister, to the League Assembly on Germany’s admission to the League.
‘Today Germany takes her seat as an equal member of this Assembly. We come not as petitioners but as partners. We bring with us no demand for revenge, but the resolve to work, with the other powers, for a peace that endures because it is just.’

Indicative content:
• Content: the speech marks Germany’s admission as an ‘equal member’ in 1926, useful evidence of the League’s gradual expansion.
• Provenance: the German Foreign Minister speaking publicly to all members; designed for both German and international audiences; reflects Stresemann’s reconciliation policy.
• Own knowledge: confirms Germany joined in 1926 after Locarno (1925); Germany would later resign in October 1933 after Hitler came to power.
• Limitation: as a public diplomatic statement it presents an idealised picture of German intentions; private German policy continued to seek treaty revision.

Indicative content:

• 1933: Hitler comes to power in Germany; both Germany and Japan resign within months over rearmament and Manchuria.

• 1937: Italy resigns after Abyssinia.
• 1939: the USSR is expelled for invading Finland; by 1939 the only great-power members are Britain and France — the League has effectively collapsed as a great-power forum on the eve of the Second World War.

lessons.title: The League's 1920s Record: Successes and Failures
lessons.description: Aaland, Upper Silesia, Vilna, Corfu and Bulgaria: where the League worked and where it didn't.
lessons.content_html:
A Mixed Record

Through the 1920s the League of Nations dealt with dozens of disputes between its members. Some were resolved quickly and quietly — useful evidence of how international arbitration could prevent war. Others exposed a structural problem the League could never escape: when one of the parties to a dispute was a great power, the unanimity rule and the absence of an army left it almost helpless. The five case studies named in the specification — Aaland Islands, Upper Silesia, Vilna, Corfu and Bulgaria — let students see this pattern in miniature.

Key Fact

Three 1920s successes: Aaland Islands (1921), Upper Silesia (1921), Bulgaria (1925). Two failures: Vilna (1920-23) and Corfu (1923). The pattern is unmistakable: the League could resolve disputes between small states; it could not handle great-power aggression.

Aaland Islands, 1921 — Success

The Aaland Islands sit in the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Finland. They were ethnically Swedish but politically part of newly independent Finland. In 1920 their population voted to join Sweden. Both governments brought the dispute to the League. The League’s commission of inquiry recommended that the islands remain part of Finland but be granted local autonomy and demilitarised. Both states accepted the ruling. The Aalands have remained autonomous Finnish territory ever since — a textbook case of arbitration working between two small, well-behaved states.

Upper Silesia, 1921 — Success

Upper Silesia was an industrial region claimed by both Germany and the new Polish state. It was ethnically mixed and economically valuable, with major coal and steel industries. The League organised a plebiscite in March 1921. Voters split — roughly 60% chose Germany, 40% Poland — and the League decided to partition the region. Germany took the larger area but Poland received the most industrially valuable part. Neither country was happy, but both accepted. The dispute was contained.

In October 1925 a frontier incident in which a Greek soldier was shot dead led to a Greek invasion of southern Bulgaria. Bulgaria appealed to the League. The Council acted swiftly: it ordered Greece to withdraw, agreed compensation of around £45,000 to be paid by Greece to Bulgaria, and threatened sanctions if Greece refused. Greece complied. The episode showed the League at its best when both states were small — and Greek diplomats privately resented being treated more harshly than Italy had been over Corfu only two years earlier.

Vilna, 1920-23 — Failure

Vilna (today’s Vilnius) was the historic capital of Lithuania but had a Polish-speaking majority. After the First World War, both Poland and the new Lithuanian state claimed it. In October 1920, Polish General Lucjan Żeligowski seized Vilna in a stage-managed ‘mutiny’, with the quiet approval of the Polish government. Lithuania appealed to the League, which condemned the seizure and called on Poland to withdraw. Poland refused.

The League had no troops to send and no appetite for sanctions against Poland, which was a key French ally against Bolshevik Russia. After three years of fruitless mediation, the League simply gave up and accepted the Polish occupation in 1923. Vilna remained Polish until the Second World War. The lesson was clear: when a member behaved badly and a great power tacitly backed it, the League had no answer.

In August 1923, an Italian general working on a Greek-Albanian border commission was murdered. Mussolini blamed Greece — without evidence — and demanded an apology and 50 million lire in compensation. When Greece refused, Mussolini ordered the bombardment and occupation of the Greek island of Corfu, killing several civilians. Greece appealed to the League. The Council was preparing to side with Greece when the dispute was suddenly transferred to the Conference of Ambassadors, an Allied body outside the League. The Conference essentially gave Mussolini what he wanted: Greece had to apologise and pay 50 million lire. Italy then withdrew from Corfu. Mussolini drew a clear lesson — the League could be sidestepped.

Humanitarian Successes Beyond the Headlines

Beyond the named case studies, the League’s specialist agencies kept working through the decade. The High Commission for Refugees, led by Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen from 1921, issued Nansen passports to hundreds of thousands of stateless people displaced by war and the Russian Civil War, and helped repatriate roughly 425,000 prisoners of war. The Health Committee fought typhus and cholera epidemics in eastern Europe and helped contain plague outbreaks in Greece. The Slavery Commission contributed to the formal end of slavery in Sierra Leone and brought international pressure on Liberia and Ethiopia. The International Labour Organization (ILO) secured 17 conventions on hours of work and the protection of women and children in industry. These successes were durable: many of these agencies would outlive the political League and form the foundation of the United Nations system created in 1945. But humanitarian work could not save the League’s political reputation in the 1930s when a great power finally tested the collective-security system.

Key Fact

The 1920s record exposed a structural exemption: when a great power was the aggressor (Italy at Corfu) or backed the aggressor (France behind Poland at Vilna), the League could not enforce its own decisions. This pattern would resurface fatally in Manchuria and Abyssinia.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on League case studies, examiners want a chain of cause and consequence, not a list. Pick one case (e.g. Vilna or Corfu) and walk through it as a sequence: trigger event → League action → great-power response → outcome → lesson learned. Use causal connectives such as ‘this led to’, ‘as a result’, ‘which meant that’ to lift the answer into the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The League had genuine 1920s successes — Aaland Islands, Upper Silesia, Bulgaria — where small states accepted arbitration.
  • It failed at Vilna (Polish seizure) and Corfu (Italian bombardment) where a great power was directly or indirectly involved.
  • Specialist agencies (ILO, Health, Refugees) achieved real humanitarian success, but the political failures of the 1920s foreshadowed the larger collapses of the 1930s.

‘The Council, having considered the report of its commission, finds that Greek troops crossed the Bulgarian frontier without justification. It calls upon Greece to withdraw all forces immediately, and orders Greece to pay £45,000 in compensation to Bulgaria for damage caused. The Council reserves the right to apply economic sanctions if Greece does not comply.’

• It ruled clearly against the aggressor — finding Greek troops had crossed without justification.

‘The Vilna affair has done us a great deal of harm. We condemned Polish action, then we accepted Polish occupation. The League cannot afford to repeat this lesson too often. If our resolutions are not enforced, what authority do they carry?’

Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a serious British insider view that the Vilna decision damaged the League’s authority. Provenance: a private letter from a leading British internationalist; likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: confirms historical record — Poland kept Vilna until 1939; the League’s climb-down weakened its credibility.
Source C — Content: a triumphant Italian framing of the League’s irrelevance to great powers. Provenance: a Mussolini-edited newspaper; designed to shape Italian and international opinion in favour of Italian assertiveness. Own knowledge: the dispute was indeed transferred to the Conference of Ambassadors; Mussolini did get the apology and 50 million lire he demanded.
Judgement: B is highly useful for measured British anxiety; C is useful as evidence of the political message Italian fascists drew, though one-sided in its framing.

Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a 1922 League of Nations report on the Aaland Islands settlement of 1921, published by the League Secretariat.
‘The Aaland question has been resolved by mediation. Both Sweden and Finland have accepted the Council’s recommendation that the islands remain Finnish but be granted autonomy and be demilitarised. The Council notes the willingness of both states to abide by international arbitration as a model for future disputes.’

Source E: An extract from a 1925 speech by French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand to the League Assembly.
‘In the past five years this League has resolved disputes that, in an earlier age, would have been settled only by war. Aaland, Upper Silesia, Bulgaria — these are the names of disputes that did not become wars because there was a Council to which states could turn. Even our failures, like Corfu, have shown the value of having such a body when others fall short.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The League of Nations was more successful than not in the 1920s.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument engaging the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear argument using both sources; judgement supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources; provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D: Aaland was a clear arbitration success.
• Source E: Briand presents a positive 1920s record — Aaland, Upper Silesia, Bulgaria.
• Specialist agencies (ILO, Health, Refugees) achieved durable humanitarian results.
• Locarno (1925) and German League entry (1926) were major political wins.
Challenging the claim:
• Vilna and Corfu were public failures involving great powers.
• Briand’s speech is partial, framed to defend the League against critics.
• The successes were small in scale; the failures involved much larger states.
• Structural weaknesses (no army, unanimity, missing US) were already visible.
Judgement: in dispute resolution between small states the League was successful; in dispute resolution involving great powers it was already failing in the 1920s, foreshadowing the 1930s collapse.

Indicative content:
• Content: gives clear evidence of small-state frustration with the League’s inability to enforce its decisions in Vilna.

• Own knowledge: confirms historical record — Poland kept Vilna throughout the inter-war period; France quietly backed Poland as an ally against the USSR; the League had no army to compel withdrawal.

lessons.title: Diplomacy Outside the League: Locarno and Kellogg-Briand
lessons.description: Stresemann’s reconciliation, the 1925 Locarno treaties and the 1928 pact that renounced war.
lessons.content_html:
A New Mood in Europe

By 1924, the worst of the post-war crisis was passing. Germany’s 1923 hyperinflation had been stabilised by Gustav Stresemann’s government with the new Rentenmark; the Dawes Plan of 1924 restructured reparations and brought American loans; and France had withdrawn its troops from the Ruhr. The result was a brief period of European optimism, often called the ‘Locarno spirit’. The 1920s reached their high-water mark of internationalism not through the League itself but through diplomacy outside it — the Locarno treaties of 1925 and the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928.

Key Fact

The Locarno treaties were signed in October 1925 by foreign ministers Gustav Stresemann (Germany), Aristide Briand (France) and Austen Chamberlain (Britain). Germany, France and Belgium voluntarily guaranteed each other’s western borders, with Britain and Italy as guarantors.

Gustav Stresemann and Reconciliation

Stresemann was the leading figure of Weimar foreign policy, serving as Chancellor briefly in 1923 and as Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in 1929. His policy was reconciliation diplomacy — cooperation with the western powers to revise the Treaty of Versailles peacefully. He calculated that confrontation would only deepen Germany’s isolation, while patient negotiation could relax reparations, end the occupation of the Ruhr, and bring Germany back into the great-power club.

It would be wrong, however, to read Stresemann as an idealistic peace-maker. His private letters show a clear-eyed strategist who wanted to recover German territory, restore German military power and undo Versailles — just by negotiation rather than force. The reconciliation was tactical. He pursued three concrete objectives: ending the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr, lifting the burden of reparations, and bringing Germany back into the great-power club through admission to the League of Nations. He used his fluent diplomatic style to build personal trust with Briand and Austen Chamberlain, while quietly continuing secret rearmament cooperation with the Soviet Union under the 1922 Treaty of Rapallo. None of this contradicted his public reconciliation policy — the two ran in parallel. Between 1924 and 1929 he successfully repositioned Germany from outlaw state to respected partner, achieving more by negotiation than the German army had achieved on the battlefield in the four years of war.

The Locarno Treaties, October 1925

Negotiations began in early 1925 in the Swiss town of Locarno. The central agreement was a western frontier guarantee: Germany, France and Belgium voluntarily accepted their existing borders as final. Britain and Italy guaranteed to act if any of the three were attacked. Germany also signed arbitration treaties with Poland and Czechoslovakia — but, crucially, did not guarantee its eastern frontiers as final.

This omission was deliberate and would matter enormously. By accepting the western borders but leaving the eastern ones open, Germany signalled that the Polish Corridor, Danzig and the Sudetenland were still subject to revision. Locarno was widely celebrated — Stresemann, Briand and Austen Chamberlain shared the 1925 Nobel Peace Prize — but it built in the very ambiguity that Hitler would exploit.

Three immediate consequences flowed from Locarno. First, in September 1926 Germany joined the League of Nations as a permanent Council member — rehabilitation completed. Second, French troops withdrew from the Rhineland zones earlier than the treaty required, the last departing in 1930 (five years ahead of schedule). Third, the ‘Locarno spirit’ encouraged broader optimism that brought the Young Plan (1929) further reducing reparations and the Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) renouncing war. For four or five years, Europe felt as if it had turned a corner.

The Kellogg-Briand Pact, 1928

The pact was a French initiative that an American Secretary of State turned into something larger. Aristide Briand initially proposed a Franco-American agreement to outlaw war between the two countries — partly as insurance against German recovery. Frank B. Kellogg, the American Secretary of State, suggested expanding it to include all states. The result, signed in Paris on 27 August 1928 by 15 countries and eventually ratified by 62, was a public renunciation of war as an instrument of national policy.

In effect, signatories pledged to settle disputes peacefully and never start a war of aggression. The pact had no enforcement mechanism — no penalties, no court, no army. Critics dismissed it from the start as ‘a kiss in the wind’. But the symbolism mattered. For the first time in history, almost every major state had publicly committed to outlawing war, providing the legal foundation that would later allow the prosecution of aggressive war as a crime at the Nuremberg trials in 1945-46.

Beneath the celebrations, three serious limits should be noted. First, eastern Europe was not protected: Germany did not commit to its frontiers with Poland and Czechoslovakia. Second, the agreement depended entirely on the personalities of the three foreign ministers; when Stresemann died in October 1929 and economic crisis followed in 1930, the Locarno spirit dissolved within months. Third, the agreement was made outside the League of Nations rather than through it, which subtly weakened the League’s status as the central body for European security — great powers preferred bilateral or multilateral deals to the unanimity-bound Council.

Key Fact

Locarno guaranteed only Germany’s western borders. Its eastern frontiers with Poland and Czechoslovakia were left open to revision. This deliberate ambiguity allowed Hitler to use the Sudetenland and the Polish Corridor as flashpoints in 1938-39.

A speech by a foreign minister at the signing is rhetorically optimistic and aimed at multiple audiences. A private memo afterwards may capture more sober calculation. Top-band answers weigh tone against context: Locarno-era public diplomacy was deliberately upbeat; the underlying calculations were often colder.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Locarno treaties of October 1925 marked the high-water mark of inter-war reconciliation, with Germany voluntarily accepting its western borders.
  • Locarno led directly to Germany’s 1926 entry into the League and to the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928, signed by 62 states renouncing war.
  • Both agreements had structural flaws: Locarno did not protect eastern borders; Kellogg-Briand had no enforcement. When economic crisis struck in 1929-30, the Locarno spirit collapsed within months.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a public speech by Aristide Briand, French Foreign Minister, at the Locarno signing ceremony, October 1925.
‘What we sign today is not merely a treaty of paper. It is a recognition that Germany and France, after fifty years of mutual fear, are partners in the rebuilding of Europe. Our western borders are now beyond dispute. Our quarrels will be resolved by arbitration, not by arms.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons why Briand presented the Locarno treaties as a turning point.

Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear points, briefly supported.
Developing: One point clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Germany and France are now ‘partners’ rather than rivals (after ‘fifty years of mutual fear’).
• The western borders are accepted as final (‘beyond dispute’).
• Disputes will be resolved by arbitration rather than war.
• It positions the treaty as a foundational shift after long Franco-German hostility.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter by Gustav Stresemann to the German ambassador to London, December 1925, drawn from the Stresemann Papers in the German Federal Archives.
‘Locarno gives us what bayonets could not: respectability and time. We have accepted the western frontiers because we cannot change them. We have left the eastern frontiers open because there our work is not finished. The Allies have what they want; we are positioned to work patiently for what we want.’

Source C: An extract from a 1925 article by Czechoslovak President Tomáš Masaryk in a Prague newspaper.
‘Germany has guaranteed her borders with France and Belgium. She has not guaranteed her borders with us, and we are told to be content with arbitration treaties. The peace settlements drew our frontiers; the Locarno spirit now hints they may yet be redrawn. The smaller states of Europe must remain on watch.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the 1925 Locarno treaties. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a candid private German calculation that Locarno is tactical, accepting the unchangeable in exchange for respectability and time. Provenance: a private letter from Stresemann to a senior diplomat; likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — Stresemann did not guarantee eastern frontiers and openly aimed to revise Versailles peacefully.
Source C — Content: a Czechoslovak warning that Locarno protects only the west and leaves successor states exposed. Provenance: a public article by the Czechoslovak president; aimed at domestic and international audiences; reflects the small-state view. Own knowledge: confirms Locarno’s asymmetry — arbitration treaties only with Poland and Czechoslovakia; the Sudetenland would later become Hitler’s lever.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German strategic thinking; C is highly useful for the small-state perspective; together they show the gap between the public ‘Locarno spirit’ and the underlying realities.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from the official text of the Kellogg-Briand Pact, signed at Paris, 27 August 1928.
‘The High Contracting Parties solemnly declare in the names of their respective peoples that they condemn recourse to war for the solution of international controversies, and renounce it as an instrument of national policy in their relations with one another. They agree that the settlement of all disputes shall never be sought except by pacific means.’

Source E: An extract from a 1928 editorial in the British satirical magazine Punch, commenting on the Kellogg-Briand Pact.
‘Sixty-two countries have signed a paper renouncing war. Not one of them has reduced an army by a single division. We have outlawed war and rearmed for it on the same morning. The pact is excellent in moral effect and modest in practical force.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘Diplomacy outside the League made the inter-war world genuinely more peaceful.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument engaging the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear argument using both sources; judgement supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources; provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D: 62 countries publicly renounced war as an instrument of policy.
• Locarno integrated Germany back into European diplomacy and led to the 1926 League entry.
• Reparations were eased through the Dawes (1924) and Young (1929) plans.
• The Locarno spirit produced a genuine reduction in tension for several years.
Challenging the claim:
• Source E: the satirical observation that signatories rearmed even as they signed.
• Kellogg-Briand had no enforcement mechanism.
• Locarno did not protect eastern Europe; Stresemann saw it as a tactical move.
• The whole structure collapsed within five years of Locarno once Stresemann died and the Depression began.
Judgement: between roughly 1924 and 1929, diplomacy outside the League did make Europe more peaceful; but the structural flaws meant the gains evaporated when economic and political conditions changed.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter by Sir Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, to his sister Hilda, just after the Locarno signing in October 1925, drawn from the Chamberlain Papers in Birmingham University Library.
‘There were tears at the table. Briand was visibly moved. Stresemann spoke as a man who had finally been given a chair at the table. I confess I felt that we had done a piece of work that may, with luck, end the wars of this century.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the diplomacy that produced the Locarno treaties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, supported by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points using content and either provenance or own knowledge.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: gives a vivid eyewitness account of the emotional atmosphere of the Locarno signing.
• Provenance: a private letter to a sibling; informal and unguarded; likely to capture genuine personal impressions.
• Own knowledge: confirms the broader picture — Locarno was widely celebrated as a turning point; Stresemann, Briand and Chamberlain shared the 1925 Nobel Peace Prize.
• Limitation: a sympathetic insider letter — Chamberlain’s optimistic tone (‘end the wars of this century’) is not corroborated by later events; the letter captures the spirit, not the underlying calculations.
