lessons.title: The Collapse of the League: Manchuria and Abyssinia
lessons.description: How the Depression and two great-power aggressions destroyed the League in the 1930s.
lessons.content_html:
Three Blows in Five Years

By 1936 the League of Nations had effectively ceased to be a serious instrument of international peace. It was killed not by a single event but by three blows landing in quick succession. First, the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 and the Great Depression that followed wrecked the cooperative international economy on which the League depended. Second, the Manchurian Crisis of 1931-33 showed the League could do nothing about Japanese aggression on a distant continent. Third, the Abyssinian Crisis of 1935-36 destroyed what remained of the League’s moral authority by exposing Britain and France privately offering Mussolini what he wanted.

Key Fact

Three blows destroyed the League: (1) the Great Depression from 1929, undermining cooperative economic action; (2) the Manchurian Crisis 1931-33, exposing the League’s impotence in Asia; (3) the Abyssinian Crisis 1935-36, destroying the League’s credibility through the Hoare-Laval Pact.

The Effects of the Depression

The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 sent shockwaves through Europe. American loans — the lifeblood of Weimar Germany since the Dawes Plan — dried up overnight. Unemployment soared: by 1932, one in three German workers, one in four British workers and one in five French workers had no job. Governments responded by raising tariffs to protect domestic industry. International trade collapsed by around 65% between 1929 and 1932. This economic nationalism destroyed the cooperative habits the League had relied on. Politically, the Depression also pushed several countries towards extremism — most fatefully Germany, where Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933.

The Manchurian Crisis, 1931-33

In September 1931 Japan’s Kwantung Army staged the ‘Mukden Incident’ — a small explosion on a Japanese-controlled railway line in Manchuria. Japan blamed the Chinese, used the ‘attack’ as a pretext, and invaded the rich resource-bearing province of Manchuria. By February 1932 the whole of Manchuria was under Japanese control and was renamed Manchukuo. China appealed to the League.

The League’s response was the Lytton Report, commissioned in December 1931 and published in October 1932. After more than a year of investigation in Manchuria, the report concluded that Japan’s action was unjustified and recommended that Manchuria become an autonomous region under Chinese sovereignty. In February 1933 the League Assembly voted 42-1 to adopt the report. Japan’s response was to walk out and resign from the League the following month. There were no economic sanctions; there was certainly no military action. Japan kept Manchukuo for the next twelve years.

Several practical reasons explain the failure. Manchuria was thousands of miles from Britain and France, and neither had the will or capacity to send a fleet. The USA, the only Pacific power capable of constraining Japan, was not a League member. The Depression made any disruption of the limited Japan trade politically toxic at home. Japan was a permanent Council member, and any sanction would have required — under the unanimity rule — Japan to vote to sanction itself. Lord Lytton’s report was a serious diplomatic document, but the League had no instrument to enforce it.

The Abyssinian Crisis, 1935-36

If Manchuria exposed the League’s impotence at distance, Abyssinia destroyed it on Europe’s doorstep. Mussolini wanted to add Abyssinia (modern Ethiopia) to Italy’s African empire as a matter of nationalist prestige and as revenge for Italy’s humiliating defeat at Adwa in 1896. A border incident at Wal Wal in December 1934 gave him a pretext. In October 1935, Italian forces invaded from Eritrea and Italian Somaliland. Emperor Haile Selassie’s troops, equipped largely with rifles and spears, were no match for Italian tanks, aircraft and mustard gas.

The League acted faster than over Manchuria, but more weakly. It declared Italy the aggressor and imposed economic sanctions in November 1935 — a ban on arms exports, financial loans and certain raw materials. Crucially, the sanctions excluded oil, coal and steel, which Italy needed most. The Suez Canal, run by a British-French company, was kept open for Italian troopships. Britain and France were unwilling to push Mussolini into the arms of Hitler — a calculation that destroyed the League’s credibility.

In December 1935, while sanctions were nominally in force, British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare and French Prime Minister Pierre Laval secretly negotiated a deal that would have given Mussolini roughly two-thirds of Abyssinia. The plan was leaked to the French press and the public outcry forced Hoare’s resignation, but the damage was done. The League’s two leading powers had been caught privately offering an aggressor most of what he wanted while publicly imposing sanctions on him. Mussolini drew the obvious lesson and continued the conquest. By May 1936 Italian forces took Addis Ababa; Haile Selassie went into exile and made his famous speech to the League Assembly in Geneva, warning ‘it is us today; it will be you tomorrow’. Sanctions were lifted in July 1936.

Why It Mattered

It is worth distinguishing the two crises clearly: in Manchuria the League had little leverage over a great power on a distant continent; in Abyssinia the League’s leading members were exposed as more interested in keeping Mussolini away from Hitler than in defending the Covenant. Hitler watched both episodes carefully. Within a year of the Abyssinian collapse he had remilitarised the Rhineland (March 1936), formed the Rome-Berlin Axis (October 1936), and concluded that the League was a paper tiger. The road from Geneva 1936 to Munich 1938 to Warsaw 1939 was short.

Key Fact

Manchuria and Abyssinia are different kinds of failure. In Manchuria the League had little practical leverage over a distant aggression. In Abyssinia the League had real leverage but Britain and France chose appeasement of Mussolini over enforcement — the Hoare-Laval Pact destroyed the League’s credibility.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on the League’s collapse, you do not need a formal introduction or conclusion to reach full marks. Examiners advise students to begin evaluating sources directly. Each source must receive a substantiated judgement on its usefulness, integrating content, provenance and your own knowledge. Reach an overall judgement that addresses the specific claim of the question rather than offering a generic ‘sources are useful in different ways’ conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Great Depression from 1929 destroyed the cooperative economic conditions on which the League depended.
  • The Manchurian Crisis 1931-33 showed the League could not act against a great power on a distant continent; Japan resigned in 1933 and kept Manchukuo.
  • The Abyssinian Crisis 1935-36 destroyed the League’s credibility when the Hoare-Laval Pact exposed Britain and France privately offering Mussolini what he wanted; Hitler drew the appropriate conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the Lytton Report on the Manchurian Crisis, presented to the League of Nations in October 1932.
‘The military operations of the Japanese troops on the night of 18-19 September 1931 cannot be regarded as measures of legitimate self-defence. The recently established Manchukuo regime cannot be regarded as having resulted from a genuine and spontaneous independence movement; it is an instrument of Japanese policy.’

Using Source A, identify two findings of the Lytton Report.

Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear points, briefly supported.
Developing: One point clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Japanese military action on 18-19 September 1931 was not legitimate self-defence.
• The new Manchukuo regime was not the result of a genuine independence movement.
• Manchukuo was an instrument of Japanese policy — a puppet state.
• Implicit finding: the Mukden Incident did not justify the invasion.

Indicative content:

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a 1936 speech to the League Assembly by Emperor Haile Selassie of Abyssinia, after Italian forces had taken Addis Ababa.
‘I, Haile Selassie I, Emperor of Ethiopia, am here today to claim that justice which is due to my people. There is no precedent for a Head of State himself speaking in this Assembly. But there is no precedent for a people being victims of such injustice. We were the first nation to call upon the League. We have been told that the League can do nothing. It is us today. It will be you tomorrow.’

Source C: An extract from a private memorandum by British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare to the British Cabinet, December 1935, drawn from the National Archives at Kew.
‘We must avoid driving Mussolini into Hitler’s arms at all costs. The Italian dictator can still be bought back. The choice before us is not between principle and expediency, but between two evils — an aggrieved Italy joined to Germany, or a partial concession that may yet keep her with us.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Abyssinian Crisis. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a moral protest by the head of state of the victim country; warns the League that its weakness puts other countries at risk. Provenance: a famous public speech to the League Assembly by Haile Selassie in 1936; designed to shame the great powers and rally world opinion. Own knowledge: Italian forces did take Addis Ababa in May 1936; sanctions were lifted in July 1936; Haile Selassie went into exile.
Source C — Content: candid British strategic calculation that Mussolini must be appeased to keep him away from Hitler. Provenance: a private memorandum to the Cabinet; likely to express genuine policy thinking; not designed for public consumption. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — the Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935 offered Mussolini around two-thirds of Abyssinia; the leak forced Hoare’s resignation; the calculation about Hitler proved miscalculated when Mussolini joined the Rome-Berlin Axis anyway in October 1936.
Judgement: B is highly useful as a moral and political document but partial; C is highly useful for the strategic calculation behind British policy but reflects only one strand of British thinking.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a 1936 article by the British journalist Geoffrey Dawson, editor of The Times, written after the Italian conquest of Abyssinia.
‘The League has not been killed by Mussolini in Africa. It has been killed by Geneva itself. Sanctions were imposed but excluded the only commodities that mattered. The Suez Canal stayed open. The Hoare-Laval plan was the moment the world saw that the League’s leading members did not believe in their own creation.’

Source E: An extract from a 1936 speech by Maxim Litvinov, Soviet Foreign Minister, to the League Assembly.
‘Comrades, the League’s structure is sound; its members are not. The Covenant has not been disproved by Manchuria or Abyssinia — it has been ignored. If the great powers will not enforce their own laws, those who broke them will not be the only ones to suffer.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The League of Nations was killed by its members rather than by its structure.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument engaging the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument using both sources; judgement supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources; provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D: argues sanctions could have worked but were deliberately weakened by Britain and France.
• Source E: argues members not structure failed.
• Hoare-Laval Pact showed leading members preferred appeasement over enforcement.
• Excluding oil from sanctions was a political choice, not a structural fact.
• Britain and France did not push for closure of the Suez Canal.
Challenging the claim:
• Structural problems were genuine: missing US, no army, unanimity rule.
• Manchuria failure was about geography and Japan’s great-power status as much as British and French choices.
• The Depression undermined cooperative economic action regardless of member willingness.
• Some structural fixes would have helped (closer Council majority voting, automatic military commitments).
Judgement: members deserve heavy blame, especially in Abyssinia; but to say the League was killed only by members understates the structural defects that made enforcement difficult from the start.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a 1933 speech by Yosuke Matsuoka, head of the Japanese delegation to the League of Nations, on Japan’s resignation from the League.
‘The Japanese government, which has consistently striven to follow the path of peace, finds itself unable to accept the report. Japan has done nothing in Manchuria that other great powers have not done elsewhere. We will not be lectured by those whose own colonies were taken by force. Japan therefore withdraws from the League.’

Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: shows the Japanese justification for resignation — the ‘great-power hypocrisy’ argument and rejection of the Lytton Report.
• Provenance: a public speech by the head of the Japanese delegation; designed for both international and Japanese domestic audiences.
• Own knowledge: confirms historical record — the Lytton Report was rejected, Japan resigned in March 1933, and Manchukuo was kept; Britain and France indeed had extensive empires acquired by force.
• Limitation: a one-sided official justification — ignores the Mukden Incident as a staged pretext.

lessons.title: Hitler's Aims and Early Foreign Policy 1933-1934
lessons.description: Hitler's foreign-policy aims, the Dollfuss Affair and the first Allied reactions, 1933-34.
lessons.content_html:
Hitler in Power

When Adolf Hitler became German Chancellor in January 1933, the world he stepped into was already shaky. The Wall Street Crash had wrecked international trade, the League of Nations was struggling with the Manchurian Crisis, and Germany’s Weimar democracy had collapsed under unemployment and political extremism. Hitler arrived with a clear set of foreign-policy aims rooted in his book Mein Kampf (1925) and in the wider Nazi belief that the Treaty of Versailles was a national humiliation that had to be undone.

Key Fact

Hitler’s foreign policy had three intertwined aims: (1) revise or destroy the Treaty of Versailles; (2) unite all German speakers in a Greater Germany; (3) win Lebensraum — living space — in eastern Europe at the expense of the Soviet Union.

The Three Aims

First came treaty revision. The 1919 settlement had stripped Germany of around 13% of its territory, restricted its army to 100,000 men, banned tanks and submarines, and forbidden union with Austria. Hitler promised to tear up these clauses one by one. Second came pan-Germanism: the idea of a single German nation including the Austrian Germans, the Sudeten Germans of Czechoslovakia, and German minorities in Poland and the Saar. This appealed to a wider Volksgemeinschaft — the Nazi ideal of a racial people’s community that crossed existing borders. Third came Lebensraum: living space in the east, to be carved out of Poland, Ukraine and European Russia, settled by German farmers and ruled by a German racial elite. The aim was openly anti-Slav and anti-communist.

These three aims were not separate boxes; they overlapped. Tearing up Versailles cleared the path for pan-German union. Pan-German union pushed Germany’s borders eastward. The eastward border made Lebensraum easier. Anti-communism justified moving against the USSR and reassured British and French conservatives who feared Bolshevism more than they feared Hitler.

First Steps in 1933

Hitler moved cautiously in 1933. Germany was militarily weak — the army was still capped at 100,000 men, and rearmament had only just begun. He used the Geneva Disarmament Conference as a stage. France refused to disarm to German levels; Hitler used this as the pretext to walk out, and in October 1933 took Germany out of both the Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations. The League made no meaningful response. This first test — would the Allies enforce the Covenant on Germany? — ended in silence.

In January 1934 Hitler signed a ten-year non-aggression pact with Poland. On the surface this looked peaceful — even surprising, given Nazi hostility to Slavs and Hitler’s long-term aims in the east. The real purpose was tactical: it broke the French alliance system in eastern Europe (France had relied on Poland to contain Germany), it bought Hitler time while he rearmed, and it presented the Nazi regime to foreign observers as a rational neighbour rather than an aggressive one. The pact was always meant to be temporary — Hitler would tear it up in 1939.

The Dollfuss Affair, July 1934

Hitler’s caution had limits. In July 1934 Austrian Nazis, encouraged from Berlin, attempted a coup in Vienna. They burst into the Chancellery, shot the Austrian Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, and proclaimed union with Germany. The coup failed: Austrian government forces crushed the Nazi rebels within hours. The decisive response, however, came not from Britain, France or the League, but from Italy. Mussolini, who had personally cultivated Dollfuss as an ally and whose family was even visiting Italy at the time, moved Italian troops to the Brenner Pass on the Austrian border and threatened intervention. Hitler, not yet ready for a confrontation, publicly disowned the rebels.

The Dollfuss Affair mattered for three reasons. It showed that Hitler was willing to interfere in a neighbour’s politics. It also showed that he would back down if a great power resisted. And it set up a paradox: in 1934 Mussolini was the obstacle to Anschluss, but within four years Mussolini would be the partner who waved it through.

Two patterns set in 1933-34 shaped what followed. Britain and France did not challenge Hitler over leaving the League or over the German-Polish pact — both fitted a wider hope that a satisfied Germany would settle down. Italy did challenge Hitler over Austria — and Hitler retreated. The lesson Hitler took was that great-power firmness worked, while moralistic League protests did not. He would now look for moves where the Allies were unlikely to push back.

Key Fact

1933-34 was a cautious testing phase. Hitler walked out of the League in October 1933 with no Allied response, signed the German-Polish Non-Aggression Pact in January 1934 to buy time, but backed down in July 1934 when Mussolini threatened intervention over the Austrian Nazi coup that killed Dollfuss.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on Hitler’s 1933-34 foreign policy, examiners reward causal links between events — not chronological listing. Aim for three or four linked events (becoming Chancellor, leaving the League, the Polish Pact, the Dollfuss Affair) connected by phrases like ‘this allowed’, ‘as a result’, or ‘because of this’. Top-band answers analyse why each step prepared the next, rather than telling the story event by event.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hitler’s foreign policy rested on three intertwined aims: revise Versailles, unite German speakers, win Lebensraum in the east.
  • In 1933 he tested the Allies by leaving the League and the Disarmament Conference; the response was silence, encouraging further moves.
  • The 1934 Austrian Nazi coup that killed Dollfuss was checked by Mussolini, not by Britain or France — teaching Hitler that great-power firmness, not League protest, decided what he could get away with.

lessons.title: The Saar, Rearmament and the Stresa Front 1935
lessons.description: The Saar, open conscription, the Stresa Front and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935.
lessons.content_html:
1935 — The Pivot Year

Of all the years between Versailles and the outbreak of war, 1935 is the pivot. In a single year Hitler won a legitimate plebiscite, openly threw off the military clauses of Versailles, watched Britain, France and Italy form a great-power coalition against him — and then watched that coalition collapse within weeks. The events of 1935 explain why later episodes (the Rhineland in 1936, Anschluss in 1938) became thinkable.

Key Fact

1935 had four key episodes: the Saar plebiscite (January), the announcement of conscription and the Luftwaffe (March), the formation of the Stresa Front (April), and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement (June).

The Saar Plebiscite, January 1935

The Saarland was a small but coal-rich German territory that Versailles had placed under League of Nations administration for fifteen years. The treaty promised that at the end of that period the inhabitants would vote on their future. In January 1935 the plebiscite was held under League supervision and the result was crushing: roughly 90% chose to return to Germany. About 9% wanted to stay under League rule and only a tiny fraction wanted union with France. The result was a genuine, internationally observed mandate. Hitler had played no part in rigging it — he simply welcomed the outcome and used it as a propaganda triumph. The Saar showed that pan-German feeling was real, not invented by the Nazis, and gave Hitler political cover to push further.

Conscription and the Luftwaffe, March 1935

In March 1935 Hitler did what every German government since 1919 had been forbidden from doing: he announced open conscription, set the army at 36 divisions (around 550,000 men), and admitted the existence of the Luftwaffe, a German air force outright banned by Versailles. The military clauses of the treaty were openly torn up. The League and the Allies protested but did not act. France, which would have to do most of the fighting, did not mobilise. Britain saw the move as a fact rather than a threat — rearmament behind closed doors had been underway since 1933 anyway.

The Stresa Front, April 1935

The shock of open rearmament briefly produced a great-power response. In April 1935 the leaders of Britain (Ramsay MacDonald), France (Pierre Laval) and Italy (Mussolini) met at Stresa on the Italian lakes. The Stresa Front condemned German rearmament, reaffirmed the Locarno guarantees, and pledged to act together against any threat to Austrian independence. For a moment, Hitler appeared isolated. The three powers that mattered most in western Europe stood against him.

On paper the Stresa Front was a serious deterrent. Britain had the largest navy in the world. France had the largest army in western Europe. Italy was Germany’s southern neighbour and had the Brenner Pass — the same border at which Mussolini had checked Hitler over Dollfuss in 1934. Together the three powers encircled Germany diplomatically. If they had stayed united, the Rhineland reoccupation a year later would have looked very different.

The Anglo-German Naval Agreement, June 1935

Within weeks the Stresa Front was undermined by Britain itself. In June 1935 London signed a bilateral naval agreement with Berlin allowing Germany a navy 35% the size of the Royal Navy — including, controversially, a submarine fleet. The British calculation was practical: rearmament was happening anyway; better to cap it by treaty than let it run unrestricted. But the political cost was huge. Britain had agreed, on its own, to legalise a major Versailles violation. France and Italy were not consulted. The signal to Hitler was that British policy was not aligned with French security concerns. The Stresa Front was holed below the waterline.

It would not survive the year. In October 1935 Mussolini invaded Abyssinia. Britain and France imposed sanctions on Italy — weak ones, but enough to push Mussolini away from his Stresa partners and toward Hitler. By the end of 1935 the great-power coalition that had briefly existed in April was gone, and Hitler had been handed three useful lessons: the Allies could not coordinate, Britain would deal bilaterally, and Italy was now in play.

Bilateral diplomacy — deals between two countries — suited Hitler in the 1930s. The League required unanimity and ran on shared principles. A bilateral deal could be done quickly with whichever country was willing, and could be presented as a face-saving compromise rather than a concession. Britain’s 1935 naval deal showed how this worked in Germany’s favour: it cut across collective Allied policy and gave Hitler legitimacy on a major point. The same tactic returned at Munich in 1938.

Key Fact

The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June 1935 was a textbook example of allied disunity: Britain unilaterally legalised a major Versailles violation, did not consult France or Italy, and broke the Stresa Front it had just signed. Hitler now had clear evidence that the Allies could not maintain a united response.

On 1935 sources, ‘own knowledge’ means dates such as January 1935 (Saar), March 1935 (conscription), April 1935 (Stresa), June 1935 (Naval Agreement). Reach a substantiated judgement on each source — do not finish with a generic ‘sources are useful in different ways’ line.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The January 1935 Saar plebiscite (90% to return to Germany) gave Hitler a legitimate, internationally observed propaganda victory.
  • In March 1935 Hitler openly broke Versailles by announcing conscription and the Luftwaffe; the League protested but did nothing.
  • The April Stresa Front briefly united Britain, France and Italy, but Britain undercut it within weeks by signing the Anglo-German Naval Agreement; Allied disunity was now Hitler’s main asset.

Judgement: A is useful as a public statement of unity but misleading on Allied solidity; B is highly useful for British strategic calculation but reflects only one strand of British and Allied thinking.

lessons.title: Escalation: Rhineland, Axis and Anti-Comintern
lessons.description: The 1936 remilitarisation of the Rhineland, the Rome-Berlin Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact.
lessons.content_html:
The Rhineland Gamble

On the morning of 7 March 1936, three battalions of German troops crossed the Rhine bridges and entered the demilitarised zone of the Rhineland. The territory was German — but Versailles had banned any German military presence west of the Rhine, and the 1925 Locarno Treaties had committed Britain, France, Italy and Germany itself to keep it that way. Hitler was tearing up two treaties at once. He privately admitted afterwards that the ‘forty-eight hours after the march into the Rhineland were the most nerve-racking in my life’. His commanders had explicit orders to retreat at once if the French Army crossed the border.

Key Fact

On 7 March 1936 Hitler reoccupied the Rhineland in defiance of both the Versailles Treaty and the 1925 Locarno Pact. German forces had orders to retreat at once if challenged, but France did not act and Britain accepted the move as Germany ‘going into its own back garden’.

Why Hitler Got Away With It

The reoccupation succeeded as a fait accompli: an action carried out so fast that opponents could not reverse it without firing first. Hitler chose the moment carefully. France was mid-election and led by a caretaker government with no appetite for war. Britain was preoccupied with the Abyssinian Crisis and reluctant to confront Germany while sanctions on Italy were unravelling. The British public mood, shaped by memories of 1914-18, leaned toward a ‘reasonable’ settlement — the Rhineland was, after all, German territory. Lord Lothian’s widely quoted remark that the Germans were ‘only going into their own back garden’ captured the prevailing British view. France could have acted alone but feared moving without British backing.

The result was a watershed. Versailles had made the demilitarised Rhineland a buffer for France — without it, German forces could now build the West Wall (Siegfried Line) facing the French frontier, a fortified line that would tie down French troops in any future conflict. Czechoslovakia and Poland, which depended on French willingness to march east in their defence, watched the moment carefully. After 1936, that defensive logic looked shakier, and the smaller central European democracies began to wonder whether French treaties were worth anything at all.

The British argument that the Rhineland was simply German territory missed the strategic point. The demilitarised zone existed not because the land was disputed (it was not) but because German forces stationed there could attack France or threaten France’s ability to defend its eastern allies. With the zone gone, France could no longer make a credible threat to march east into Germany if Hitler attacked Poland or Czechoslovakia. The whole French alliance system in eastern Europe rested on a buffer that disappeared on 7 March 1936.

The Rome-Berlin Axis, October 1936

The collapse of the Stresa Front in 1935 had pushed Mussolini away from Britain and France. By autumn 1936 the two dictators had begun to align openly. In October 1936, Italy and Germany signed agreements covering Austria, the Balkans, Spain and economic cooperation. Mussolini’s public speech in Milan on 1 November 1936 referred for the first time to the ‘Axis’ between Rome and Berlin around which European affairs would now turn. The Axis was not yet a military alliance — that came in 1939 with the Pact of Steel — but it locked in a new diplomatic geometry. Britain and France faced one fascist bloc, not two separate threats.

The Anti-Comintern Pact, November 1936

Within weeks of the Axis announcement, Germany signed a separate agreement with Japan: the Anti-Comintern Pact of 25 November 1936. The pact was framed as a defensive arrangement against the Communist International (Comintern), the Soviet-led organisation that coordinated communist parties around the world. Italy joined in November 1937. The pact mattered for two reasons. It was openly anti-Soviet, which appealed to British and French conservatives who feared Bolshevism more than Nazism. And it linked the European fascist powers with Japan — meaning that any future European war would now have a Pacific dimension.

The Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact were powered by genuine ideological alignment, not just shared interests. All three powers — Nazi Germany, fascist Italy and militarist Japan — opposed parliamentary democracy, communism, and what they called ‘international finance’. All three saw themselves as ‘have-not’ nations entitled to expand at the expense of decadent empires. Cooperation in Spain (where German and Italian forces fought for Franco from 1936) and in propaganda showed the alignment in action. By the end of 1936 Hitler had moved from diplomatic isolation to leadership of a fascist bloc.

Key Fact

1936 transformed Europe’s diplomatic balance. The March Rhineland reoccupation showed Britain and France would not act; the October Rome-Berlin Axis aligned Hitler with Mussolini; the November Anti-Comintern Pact added Japan. By the year’s end Hitler led a fascist bloc Britain and France had to confront together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on 1936, examiners reward causal links between the three episodes (Rhineland, Axis, Anti-Comintern), not three separate stories. Use connective phrases like ‘because of this’, ‘encouraged by’, ‘this allowed’, to show how the Rhineland made Mussolini’s alignment easier and how the Axis prepared the ground for the Anti-Comintern Pact. Pin events to months (March, October, November) for precision.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • On 7 March 1936 Hitler reoccupied the Rhineland with a small force ordered to retreat if challenged; France did not act and Britain accepted the move.
  • The Rome-Berlin Axis of October 1936 aligned Mussolini with Hitler, ending the great-power isolation that had briefly existed in 1935.
  • The Anti-Comintern Pact of November 1936 added Japan to the fascist diplomatic bloc and gave any future European war a global dimension.

Source B — Content: a candid British Cabinet view that the breach was clear but military response was politically impossible. lessons.title: Anschluss and the Reasons for Appeasement
lessons.description: The 1938 union with Austria and the reasons Britain chose appeasement as its main response.
lessons.content_html:
Anschluss, March 1938

In March 1938 Hitler annexed Austria without firing a shot and without any meaningful Allied response. The pressure had been building since 1934, when the Austrian Nazi attempt to assassinate Chancellor Dollfuss had failed only because Mussolini had moved Italian troops to the Brenner Pass. Four years on, the diplomatic balance had shifted. The Rome-Berlin Axis (October 1936) had aligned Mussolini with Hitler, removing the southern obstacle. The Allies had absorbed the Rhineland reoccupation. Anschluss, banned by Versailles in 1919, was now within Hitler’s reach.

Key Fact

Anschluss came in three stages: the Berchtesgaden meeting (12 February 1938) where Schuschnigg was bullied into Nazi appointments; the cancelled Austrian plebiscite (9 March); and the Wehrmacht entry into Austria (12 March). A staged plebiscite in April recorded an official 99% in favour of union.

From Berchtesgaden to Vienna

In February 1938 Hitler summoned the Austrian Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg to his Alpine retreat at Berchtesgaden. Schuschnigg was kept waiting and then forced to accept a series of demands: the appointment of the Austrian Nazi Arthur Seyss-Inquart as Interior Minister with control of the police, an amnesty for jailed Nazis, and an effective veto for Berlin over Austrian foreign policy. Schuschnigg returned home and tried to fight back. On 9 March he announced a plebiscite on Austrian independence, to be held within four days. The hurried timing was meant to outflank Hitler — an honest vote would almost certainly have rejected union.

Hitler responded by demanding the plebiscite be cancelled and Schuschnigg replaced. On 11 March the Austrian government collapsed; Seyss-Inquart took over and immediately invited German troops in to ‘preserve order’. On the morning of 12 March 1938, the Wehrmacht crossed the Austrian border without resistance. Hitler made a triumphal entry into Vienna two days later. A retrospective plebiscite in April 1938 was conducted under Nazi conditions and recorded an official 99% in favour of union — a result that no observer treated as honest, though there was undoubtedly genuine pan-German enthusiasm in many areas.

The British government issued formal protests but took no action. France was without a government for several days during the crisis. Mussolini, who had stopped Hitler in 1934, this time accepted the move without resistance — Hitler thanked him in person, declaring ‘I shall never forget this’. Anthony Eden had already resigned as British Foreign Secretary in February 1938, partly over Chamberlain’s willingness to negotiate with the dictators. The new Foreign Secretary, Lord Halifax, accepted Anschluss as a regrettable but practical reality.

Why Britain Chose Appeasement

By 1938 Neville Chamberlain’s policy of appeasement was settled. Modern historians stress that this was a rational policy given Britain’s position, not the moral failure or cowardice that the wartime ‘Guilty Men’ (Cato, 1940) charge later painted. Chamberlain’s reasoning rested on six interlocking pressures.

First, military weakness. British rearmament had only begun in earnest in 1936-37 and key systems — radar, fighter aircraft, anti-aircraft guns — were not yet ready in 1938. The Chiefs of Staff repeatedly warned the Cabinet that war that year carried a serious risk of defeat. Second, imperial overstretch: the Royal Navy faced potential threats from Germany in the North Sea, Italy in the Mediterranean, and Japan in the Far East — impossible to meet all three. Third, public pacifism: the memory of 1914-18 was still raw, and the 1933 Oxford Union vote refusing ‘to fight for King and Country’ reflected a wider mood. Fourth, allies were thin: the United States was isolationist after the 1935 Neutrality Acts, and Stalin’s USSR was distrusted across the political class. Fifth, Empire and Commonwealth opinion: the Dominions (Canada, Australia, South Africa) had told London they would not fight a European war that looked unjustified to them. Sixth, the sincere belief that Hitler had real grievances which could be met by negotiation — revising Versailles, returning ethnic Germans, allowing reasonable rearmament — without a second world war.

Two schools of historians have argued over Chamberlain’s policy. The wartime ‘Guilty Men’ tradition, launched by the pamphlet of that name in 1940, presented appeasement as moral cowardice and Chamberlain as personally responsible for the war. The post-1960s revisionist tradition (Reynolds, McDonough) stresses the constraints Chamberlain faced and treats appeasement as a rational policy that bought time for rearmament. Most modern historians sit between these poles: Chamberlain’s situation was genuinely difficult, but his personal confidence in face-to-face dealings with Hitler was a serious error of judgement. Examiners reward students who present these as competing interpretations rather than picking one.

Key Fact

British appeasement rested on six pressures: military weakness in 1938, imperial overstretch facing three potential enemies, public pacifism after 1918, the absence of strong allies (USA isolationist, USSR distrusted), Dominion opinion, and Chamberlain’s belief that Hitler’s grievances could be settled by negotiation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on Anschluss or appeasement, you do not need a formal introduction or conclusion to reach full marks. Begin evaluating sources directly. Each source must receive a substantiated judgement integrating content, provenance and your own knowledge. The overall judgement must address the specific claim of the question — for example, whether appeasement was rational policy or moral failure — rather than offering a generic ‘sources are useful in different ways’ line. Examiners reward students who present the ‘Guilty Men’ vs revisionist debate as competing interpretations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Anschluss in March 1938 annexed a sovereign state without resistance: Schuschnigg was bullied at Berchtesgaden, the planned plebiscite cancelled, and the Wehrmacht entered Austria on 12 March.
  • Mussolini, who had stopped Hitler in 1934, accepted Anschluss in 1938 because the Rome-Berlin Axis had realigned Italian foreign policy.
  • British appeasement was a rational policy given six pressures — military weakness, imperial overstretch, public pacifism, weak allies, Dominion opinion, and the belief that Hitler’s grievances could be negotiated — though historians remain split between ‘Guilty Men’ and revisionist readings.

• B: a private memorandum, expressing genuine policy thinking, not designed for public consumption.
• C: a polemical wartime pamphlet written for a public looking for someone to blame.
• D: a modern academic article with the benefit of hindsight and archival access.
Judgement: appeasement was a rational response to severe constraints, but not all of it was: the personal misjudgement of Hitler’s reliability and the abandonment of Czechoslovakia were errors that the rational case alone cannot defend.

lessons.title: The Sudeten Crisis and Munich
lessons.description: Henlein, the September 1938 crisis, the Munich Agreement and 'peace for our time'.
lessons.content_html:
The Sudeten Pretext

Czechoslovakia was the strongest democracy in central Europe in 1938 — a well-armed state of about 15 million people with French and Soviet defensive treaties. Yet within months of Anschluss it had been carved up at a four-power conference where its own representatives were not present. The pretext was the Sudetenland, a mountainous border region containing about three million ethnic Germans — and crucially, Czechoslovakia’s defensive fortifications. Hitler used the principle of national self-determination, championed by Wilson at Versailles, as cover for what was in reality a strategic move against the Czechoslovak state.

Key Fact

The Sudeten Crisis came to a head in three Chamberlain-Hitler meetings: Berchtesgaden (15 September 1938), Bad Godesberg (22 September), and the Munich Conference (29-30 September). The Sudetenland was transferred to Germany; Czechoslovakia was not at the table.

Henlein and the Sudeten German Party

From early 1938 the Sudeten German Party, led by Konrad Henlein, ramped up demands for autonomy. Henlein had been instructed by Hitler in March 1938 to make demands the Czech government could never accept — ensuring the agitation would continue regardless of any concession. The Czech President Edvard Beneš offered a series of concessions through the spring and summer; each time Henlein raised the bar. By August 1938 the situation was at a deliberate boiling point. In May 1938 the Czech government had ordered partial mobilisation in response to false rumours of German troop movements; the ‘May Crisis’ showed the Czechs would resist, but also showed Hitler that mobilisation was politically expensive.

On 12 September 1938 Hitler delivered a speech at the Nuremberg Rally demanding self-determination for the Sudeten Germans — effectively a demand to be allowed to take the territory. Riots broke out across the Sudetenland. The Czech government declared martial law. War in central Europe looked imminent.

Three Meetings, Three Stages

Chamberlain, sixty-nine and never having flown before, took the dramatic step of flying to meet Hitler personally. The shuttle diplomacy across September 1938 came in three stages:

15 September: Berchtesgaden. At Hitler’s mountain retreat, Chamberlain accepted the principle that the Sudetenland should be transferred to Germany on grounds of self-determination. He flew home to consult Cabinet and Paris; Beneš was effectively informed by his allies that the territory was lost.

22 September: Bad Godesberg. Hitler now raised the demands. Transfer must happen immediately, by military occupation, with no plebiscites and no orderly handover. Chamberlain refused. The Czechs and the French began preparing for war; the Royal Navy was mobilised; gas masks were distributed to British schoolchildren.

29-30 September: Munich. Mussolini, alarmed at the prospect of war, proposed a four-power conference. Britain, France, Germany and Italy met at Munich. Czechoslovakia was not invited; Beneš was kept in an antechamber and informed of the result. The agreement followed Hitler’s Bad Godesberg demands almost in full. The Sudetenland was transferred to Germany over ten days from 1 October. Czechoslovakia lost its border fortifications, around a third of its industrial capacity, and most of its strategic depth. Slovakia and Ruthenia gained autonomy. The Polish government opportunistically seized the Teschen district; Hungary took further border areas.

The exclusion of Czechoslovakia from the conference deciding its fate is one of the most criticised features of Munich. Chamberlain and Daladier reasoned that the alternative was war, and that Czechoslovakia’s consent was unobtainable but unnecessary if Britain and France would not fight to defend it. The result was an abandonment of an ally that Czechoslovakia, France’s formal treaty partner since 1924, never forgave. Beneš resigned and went into exile. The Czech army, which had been ready to fight, was not consulted.

‘Peace for Our Time’

Returning from Munich on 30 September, Chamberlain produced a separate Anglo-German declaration that he and Hitler had signed that morning — the famous ‘piece of paper’. Standing at 10 Downing Street he announced ‘peace for our time’, drawing parallels with Disraeli’s 1878 return from Berlin. Most British and French opinion welcomed the agreement: war had been avoided. There were dissenting voices — Churchill called it ‘a defeat without a war’ — but for the moment the relief was overwhelming. Chamberlain genuinely believed he had bought lasting peace, not merely time. The events of March 1939 would show how badly that judgement was misplaced.

A common student error is to write that Munich gave Hitler Czechoslovakia. It did not. The Munich Agreement transferred the Sudetenland alone — the German-speaking border region. The rest of Czechoslovakia, now indefensible without its border fortifications, remained a separate state. It was Hitler’s seizure of the rump Czech lands in March 1939, not Munich, that ended Czech independence and ended British appeasement. Examiners report this confusion as a recurring error in narrative accounts.

Key Fact

Munich transferred the Sudetenland only — the rest of Czechoslovakia remained a state, but without its mountain fortifications and a third of its industry. The famous ‘piece of paper’ promised future Anglo-German consultation. Hitler’s seizure of the rump Czech lands the following March, not Munich itself, ended British appeasement.

Distinguish carefully between the Sudetenland (transferred at Munich) and Czechoslovakia (occupied in March 1939) — examiners report frequent chronological confusion here. Reach a substantiated judgement on each source rather than a generic ‘sources are useful in different ways’ conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Henlein’s Sudeten German Party agitated through 1938 under Berlin’s instructions; Hitler used self-determination as a pretext for what was a strategic move against Czechoslovakia.
  • The September 1938 crisis ran through three meetings — Berchtesgaden, Bad Godesberg and Munich — with Czechoslovakia kept out of the room at every stage.
  • Munich transferred the Sudetenland only; Chamberlain returned with the ‘piece of paper’ promising peace, but the rump Czech state had lost its fortifications and was now indefensible.

Study Source A.

practice_questions.text:
Study Sources B and C.

Source B: An extract from a 1938 newspaper report on Chamberlain’s return to 10 Downing Street, holding the Anglo-German declaration signed at Munich.
‘The Prime Minister waved the famous piece of paper before a delighted London crowd. “My good friends,” he said, “this is the second time in our history that there has come back from Germany to Downing Street peace with honour. I believe it is peace for our time.”’

Source C: An extract from a 1938 private memorandum by President Edvard Beneš of Czechoslovakia, written shortly after the Munich Conference, drawn from the Beneš archive in Prague.
‘We have been betrayed by friends to whom we owed loyalty. France was bound to us by treaty since 1924; she has not honoured it. Britain spoke of self-determination but applied it only on the German side. We were not at the table where our country was divided. We have lost the fortifications, the industry, the strategic depth. The state will not survive.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Munich Agreement. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a celebratory British public scene as Chamberlain announces ‘peace for our time’. Provenance: a contemporary newspaper report designed for British readers, capturing public mood at a single moment. Own knowledge: confirms the historical record — Chamberlain genuinely believed he had bought lasting peace; British and French opinion was overwhelmingly relieved; Churchill’s ‘defeat without a war’ verdict was a minority view.
Source C — Content: the bitter Czech presidential view that Britain and France had abandoned a treaty ally and divided the country in its absence. Provenance: a private memorandum by the Czechoslovak President; not designed for public consumption; reflects the perspective of the country most directly harmed. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — France had a treaty obligation to Czechoslovakia from 1924; Czechoslovakia was not at the conference; the Sudetenland contained the country’s mountain fortifications and a third of its industry; Beneš resigned shortly afterwards.
Judgement: B is useful as a snapshot of British public reaction but partial — it reflects relief, not strategic judgement; C is highly useful for the Czech perspective and for the practical consequences, but reflects a national grievance and not the wider picture of British constraints.

lessons.title: The End of Appeasement: Prague and the Polish Guarantee
lessons.description: How the March 1939 occupation of Czechoslovakia and the Polish guarantee changed British policy.
lessons.content_html:
The Hinge Moment

Munich had transferred the Sudetenland in October 1938. Six months later, on 15 March 1939, German troops marched into Prague and seized what was left of Czechoslovakia. Bohemia and Moravia became a German ‘protectorate’ under Reich administration; Slovakia became a German puppet state under the priest-politician Jozef Tiso. Hitler personally toured Prague Castle that night. The action was unmistakably different from what had gone before. The seized populations were Czech, not German. The principle of self-determination — Hitler’s constant pretext since 1933 — could not be made to fit. Within two weeks British policy had changed.

Key Fact

The end of appeasement came in two weeks. On 15 March 1939 German troops entered Prague. On 17 March Chamberlain’s Birmingham speech publicly turned. On 31 March Britain announced the Polish guarantee. France joined within days, and on 7 April Mussolini invaded Albania.

15 March 1939: Prague

The Czech President Emil Hácha — who had replaced Beneš after Munich — was summoned to Berlin overnight on 14-15 March. Hitler kept him waiting until 1 a.m. and then presented him with the choice: sign acceptance of a German ‘protectorate’ or watch Prague be bombed at dawn. Hácha reportedly suffered a heart attack during the meeting and was kept conscious by injections from Hitler’s personal physician. He signed. German troops entered Prague at 6 a.m. on 15 March. Slovakia, encouraged by Berlin to declare independence the day before, became a satellite state. The whole of Czechoslovakia was gone.

The British Public Turn

In Britain, the public reaction was sharper than anything since 1935. Munich had been welcomed because it had appealed to a principle — self-determination — and avoided war. Prague could not be defended on either ground. The Times, which had backed Munich, turned. Conservative MPs who had cheered Chamberlain in October 1938 now openly questioned the policy. Lord Halifax, who as Foreign Secretary had accepted Anschluss with regret in March 1938, told Chamberlain bluntly that the policy had run out. Chamberlain’s personal credibility was on the line. On 17 March, in a speech at Birmingham marking his seventieth birthday, he made the public turn. Britain, he said, would resist any further German moves toward European domination.

The Birmingham speech of 17 March 1939 is sometimes called the moment Chamberlain ‘abandoned appeasement’. The reality is more nuanced. Chamberlain still hoped to avoid war, but he now publicly accepted that Hitler could not be trusted to honour an agreement — the central premise of Munich. The shift from negotiation to deterrence followed within two weeks. The policy that had defined British foreign policy since 1937 was over in everything but name.

31 March 1939: The Polish Guarantee

Hitler had begun openly pressing Poland for the return of Danzig — the Free City under League administration — and for an extraterritorial corridor across Polish territory linking Germany to East Prussia. Poland refused. On 31 March 1939 Chamberlain told the House of Commons that Britain would lend Poland ‘all support in their power’ in the event of any threat to Polish independence. France joined the guarantee within days. Greece and Romania received similar guarantees in April. The strategic shift was complete: Britain and France had moved from negotiation to deterrence.

Historians have long argued over whether the guarantee was militarily credible. Britain and France had no direct way of defending Poland; their best hope of relieving German pressure was a Western Front offensive that neither was militarily ready to launch. The guarantee made political sense as a deterrent — signalling to Hitler that any Polish move would mean war — but it could not stop a German invasion in practice. The guarantee’s real purpose was therefore to deter, not to defend. When Hitler called the bluff in September 1939, Britain and France honoured their promise but could not save Poland.

Conscription and Mussolini in Albania

In April 1939 Britain introduced peacetime conscription — the first time outside a major war — signalling to Berlin that the rearmament effort had moved into a new phase, with men as well as money committed to the coming confrontation. On 7 April 1939 Mussolini opportunistically invaded Albania, taking advantage of European attention focused on Poland. The Italian move did not provoke a major Allied response — Britain and France were focused on the German threat — but it confirmed that the Axis powers were now acting in coordination, and prompted further British guarantees to Greece and Romania later in the month to deter any Italian move toward the Balkans.

Key Fact

March 1939 was the hinge moment. Munich had been defensible on grounds of self-determination; Prague could not be. The seizure of non-German Czech lands ended the policy of appeasement and produced the Polish guarantee, peacetime conscription and a public shift to deterrence.

Top-band answers explain why the seizure of non-German territory destroyed the moral case for appeasement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • On 15 March 1939 German troops occupied Prague; Bohemia and Moravia became a Reich protectorate, Slovakia a German puppet, and the principle of self-determination could no longer cover Hitler’s actions.
  • British public opinion turned within days; Chamberlain’s Birmingham speech of 17 March publicly abandoned the trust on which Munich had rested.
  • On 31 March Britain guaranteed Poland; France followed; peacetime conscription was introduced in April; Mussolini invaded Albania the same month. Appeasement was over.

practice_questions.text: Study Sources B and C. Source B: An extract from a 1939 private memorandum by Lord Halifax, British Foreign Secretary, to the Cabinet, drawn from the National Archives at Kew. ‘The argument for further negotiation has run out. Czechoslovakia was not a German-speaking population; the principle of self-determination cannot be invoked. Public opinion has changed and so must our policy. We must move from concession to deterrence; the Polish guarantee is the means.’ Source C: An extract from a 1939 leading article in The Times, written shortly after the German occupation of Prague. ‘Six months ago this newspaper supported the Munich Agreement on its merits. We do not regret that judgement, given the case as it then stood. But the German action of 15 March is a different matter. The seizure of a Slav population destroys the foundation of appeasement. Trust has not been broken; it never existed.’ Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the end of British appeasement. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each. Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made. Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit. Emerging: Description or accusations of bias. Indicative content: Source B — Content: a candid Cabinet rationale for moving from negotiation to deterrence; identifies self-determination as the failed argument. Provenance: a private memorandum to the Cabinet by the Foreign Secretary; reflects genuine policy thinking; not for public consumption. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — Halifax did push the policy turn after Prague; the Polish guarantee followed on 31 March. Source C — Content: a major British newspaper turning against the policy it had previously supported; treats Prague as the watershed. Provenance: a contemporary newspaper editorial designed to influence public and political opinion. Own knowledge: The Times had been a leading supporter of appeasement under Geoffrey Dawson; its turn was a significant signal in British political culture. Judgement: B is useful for the high-level Cabinet calculation; C is useful for the public mood and the role of the press in shaping it. Together they capture the joint shift in elite and public opinion that ended appeasement.

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways in which the March 1939 occupation of Czechoslovakia was different from the September 1938 transfer of the Sudetenland.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct ways clearly explained with precise context.
Secure: Two clear ways with relevant detail.
Developing: One way developed; second weak.
Emerging: General comment.

Indicative content:
• Justification: the Sudetenland transfer could be defended on grounds of self-determination because the population was German; the March 1939 occupation involved a Slav population that could not be claimed for the Reich on those grounds.
• Method: the Sudetenland was transferred under a four-power agreement signed at Munich; the March 1939 occupation was unilateral, secured by overnight pressure on Hácha and military entry without conference.
• Allied response: the Sudetenland transfer was accepted as ‘peace for our time’; the March 1939 occupation triggered Chamberlain’s Birmingham speech and the Polish guarantee within two weeks.
• Effect on policy: Munich extended appeasement; March 1939 ended it.

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways in which the British guarantee to Poland of 31 March 1939 was useful as a deterrent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points with relevant detail.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Public signal: the guarantee committed Britain in advance to defending Polish independence, reversing the previous policy of avoiding eastern European entanglements; Hitler could no longer assume Britain would stay out.
• Strategic clarity: by joining Britain to Poland and being followed by France within days, the guarantee built a continental coalition; Hitler now had to plan for a two-front war.
• Domestic effect: the guarantee was followed by peacetime conscription in April 1939, signalling that British rearmament had moved into a new phase.
• Limitation: the guarantee could not in practice defend Poland from invasion; Britain and France had no way of relieving German pressure on Polish territory in 1939, as September would prove.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the German occupation of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 ended the policy of appeasement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons clearly explained with precise context and evidence; implications drawn out. Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail. Developing: Two reasons identified, only one developed. Emerging: Reasons listed without explanation. Indicative content: • The principle of self-determination — Hitler’s constant pretext since 1933 — could not be applied to a Slav population. The seizure of non-German territory destroyed the moral case for appeasement and the assumption that German aims could be settled by treaty revision. • Trust in Hitler’s word collapsed: Munich had committed Hitler not to take further European territory; the Prague occupation was a deliberate breach within six months. Chamberlain’s personal authority depended on Hitler honouring the agreement; once that was gone, the policy could not continue. • British public opinion turned: The Times, which had backed Munich, turned against the policy; Conservative MPs who had cheered Chamberlain in October 1938 now demanded a change. • Strategic logic shifted: the loss of the rump Czech state opened central Europe to German power and exposed Poland as the next target; deterrence through the Polish guarantee replaced negotiation.

lessons.title: Nazi-Soviet Pact, Poland and the Outbreak of War
lessons.description: The Nazi-Soviet Pact, the invasion of Poland and responsibility for the outbreak of war.
lessons.content_html:
A Diplomatic Revolution

For most of the 1930s, Hitler and Stalin had presented one another as ideological enemies. Nazism rested on militant anti-communism; the Soviet Union had built the Comintern to fight fascism. The Anti-Comintern Pact of 1936 had been openly aimed at Moscow. So when, on the night of 23 August 1939, Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov signed a non-aggression pact in the Kremlin, the world was stunned. The Nazi-Soviet Pact reversed every assumption of European diplomacy. It is one of the clearest examples of a diplomatic revolution in twentieth-century history.

Key Fact

August-September 1939 saw four hinge events: Anglo-French-Soviet talks failed in mid-August; the Nazi-Soviet Pact was signed on 23 August; Germany invaded Poland on 1 September; Britain and France declared war on 3 September. Soviet forces entered eastern Poland on 17 September.

Why Stalin Signed

Stalin’s motives were practical, not ideological. Soviet diplomacy through summer 1939 had pursued two tracks at once. From April, Britain and France had been negotiating a tripartite alliance with Moscow against further German aggression. The talks dragged. Britain sent only a junior delegation by the slowest route. The Western powers refused to put pressure on Poland to permit Soviet troops to cross Polish territory in any future war — meaning the Red Army could not actually fight Germany on the eastern front. Stalin concluded the British and French were not serious. Meanwhile Hitler, who needed an eastern flank secured before invading Poland, offered Stalin terms the Western powers could not match: a non-aggression pact, territorial gains in eastern Europe, and time. The deal was signed on 23 August 1939.

A secret protocol divided eastern Europe into spheres of influence. Germany would take western Poland; the USSR would take eastern Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Bessarabia (later modified to include Lithuania). The protocol was hidden from the public; it remained denied by Moscow until 1989.

Britain and France had genuine reasons to hesitate. The British political class distrusted Stalin’s purges, his record on collectivisation, and the Comintern’s role in fomenting communist movements abroad. The Polish government, with bitter memories of the 1920 Soviet-Polish War, refused to allow Soviet troops on Polish soil. Yet the slowness was striking: the British naval mission to Moscow took five days by passenger ship while Ribbentrop flew to Moscow in a single afternoon. Stalin’s judgement that the West was buying time, not seriously seeking an alliance, was not unreasonable. Historians remain divided on whether a serious British effort in spring 1939 could have produced a different outcome.

1 September: Poland

With his eastern flank secured, Hitler launched the invasion of Poland at 4:45 a.m. on 1 September 1939. The German armed forces deployed the new Blitzkrieg tactics — armoured columns supported by close air support and motorised infantry — that would later overrun France. The Polish army, although large, was poorly equipped to face this combination. Britain and France issued an ultimatum demanding immediate withdrawal. Hitler ignored it. On 3 September 1939, Britain and France declared war.

On 17 September 1939, Soviet forces invaded eastern Poland from the east, in line with the secret protocol. By the end of September, Poland had ceased to exist as a state. Britain and France had honoured their guarantee, but they had no realistic way of helping Poland militarily; the Anglo-French expectation was that the war would be long and decided in the west.

Responsibility for the War

Examiners ask students to weigh responsibility for the outbreak of war among Hitler, Stalin and Chamberlain. There is no single answer; the highest-band responses present these as competing arguments rather than picking one and ignoring the others.

Hitler is the prime mover. Every territorial action between 1933 and 1939 had been a German one: leaving the League, rearmament, the Rhineland, Anschluss, the Sudetenland, Prague, Danzig. The historian A.J.P. Taylor controversially argued in The Origins of the Second World War (1961) that Hitler was an opportunist exploiting circumstances rather than a master planner executing a step-by-step programme. Most modern historians sit between Taylor and the older ‘intentionalist’ view: Hitler was both opportunist and planner. The 1939 invasion of Poland was a deliberate German choice.

Stalin is an opportunist. The Nazi-Soviet Pact removed the eastern obstacle that might have deterred Hitler. Stalin gained territory in eastern Poland, the Baltic states and Bessarabia, and bought time to build up the Red Army. The pact made the September invasion possible in its actual form — Hitler would not have moved without it. Stalin shares responsibility for enabling the immediate trigger, but did not start the war.

Chamberlain represents the failure of British policy. The wartime ‘Guilty Men’ tradition (Cato, 1940) blamed appeasement for emboldening Hitler. The revisionist tradition (Reynolds, McDonough) stresses that he faced real constraints and bought time for British rearmament. Most modern historians treat appeasement as a rational response to those constraints that nonetheless made costly errors — especially Munich, the abandonment of Czechoslovakia, and the slowness of the 1939 Moscow negotiations.

The historiographical debate over Hitler’s 1933-39 foreign policy is between ‘intentionalists’ (Hitler had a master plan from Mein Kampf onwards) and ‘structuralists’ (Hitler was an opportunist exploiting circumstances). A.J.P. Taylor was the first major historian to argue the structuralist case. Most modern historians draw on both traditions: the broad goals (treaty revision, pan-Germanism, Lebensraum) were consistent, but the particular moves and the timing reflected opportunity. Examiners reward students who present the debate as competing interpretations rather than picking one and ignoring the other.

Key Fact

Responsibility for war can be weighed across three figures. Hitler was the prime mover — every territorial action 1933-39 was German. Stalin was an opportunist who enabled the trigger via the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Chamberlain represents the failure of appeasement, though historians remain divided on whether his policy was rational or cowardly.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on responsibility for war, you do not need a formal introduction or conclusion to reach full marks. Begin evaluating sources directly. The overall judgement must address the specific claim of the question; examiners reward students who present Hitler, Stalin and Chamberlain as competing arguments rather than picking one. Reference the Taylor ‘intentionalist vs opportunist’ debate where relevant, and the ‘Guilty Men’ vs revisionist split on appeasement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 23 August 1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact reversed years of ideological hostility; its secret protocol divided eastern Europe between Berlin and Moscow.
  • Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war on 3 September; Soviet forces entered Poland from the east on 17 September.
  • Responsibility for war is best weighed across Hitler (prime mover), Stalin (opportunist who enabled the trigger), and Chamberlain (whose appeasement failed); historians remain split between intentionalist and structuralist readings of Hitler’s policy.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the public text of the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939 by Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov.
‘The two Contracting Parties undertake to refrain from any act of force, any aggressive action and any attack against one another, whether individually or jointly with other Powers. In the event of either Party becoming the object of warlike action by a third Power, the other Party shall in no manner lend its support to this third Power.’

Using Source A, identify two terms of the Nazi-Soviet Pact.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded terms with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear terms, briefly supported.
Developing: One term clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific terms.

Indicative content:
• Both parties undertook to refrain from any act of force or aggressive action against one another.
• Both parties undertook not to support any third power that attacked the other.
• The agreement applied whether the action was individual or jointly with other powers.
• Implicit term: the public text contained no reference to the secret protocol dividing eastern Europe.

practice_questions.text: Study Sources B, C and D. Source B: An extract from a 1939 private memorandum by Joseph Stalin to his Politburo, drawn from the Soviet archives released after 1989. ‘The Anglo-French talks have produced nothing. They send junior officials by slow boat. They will not press the Poles to permit Red Army transit. We are being asked to fight for what they will not defend. Berlin offers what the West refuses: a pact, time, and territory. We will sign.’ Source C: An extract from a 1939 BBC broadcast by Neville Chamberlain on the morning of 3 September 1939, declaring war on Germany. ‘This morning the British Ambassador in Berlin handed the German government a final note stating that, unless we heard from them by eleven o’clock, that they were prepared at once to withdraw their troops from Poland, a state of war would exist between us. I have to tell you now that no such undertaking has been received, and that consequently this country is at war with Germany.’ Source D: An extract from a 1961 academic article by the British historian A.J.P. Taylor in The Origins of the Second World War. ‘Hitler had no master plan. He was an opportunist who exploited circumstances. The other powers, by their actions and their failures, made his programme possible. He took Poland not because he had always meant to, but because the path was open and the Pact secured his rear.’ Write an essay on the question: ‘Hitler bore overwhelming responsibility for the outbreak of war in September 1939.’ Using Sources B, C and D and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument engaging the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from all three sources; substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument using all three sources; judgement supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to sources; provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source C: Chamberlain’s broadcast attaches the start of war specifically to Hitler’s refusal to withdraw from Poland.
• Own knowledge: every territorial action 1933-39 was German — League withdrawal, rearmament, Rhineland, Anschluss, Sudetenland, Prague, Danzig demand.
• The 1 September 1939 invasion was a deliberate German choice.
Challenging or qualifying the claim:
• Source B: Stalin’s pact removed the eastern obstacle and made the September invasion possible in its actual form.
• Source D: Taylor argues Hitler was an opportunist whom others enabled; not a sole master planner.
• Own knowledge: Western failure in 1939 Moscow talks; the slowness of the British delegation; British acceptance of repeated German moves through 1936-38; the ‘Guilty Men’ reading of appeasement.
Provenance points:
• B: a private archival memorandum, expressing genuine policy thinking; revealed only after 1989.
• C: a public broadcast designed to rally a nation at the moment of declaration.
• D: a controversial academic re-evaluation by a leading historian.
Judgement: Hitler bore the prime responsibility — the active aggression was always German — but Stalin’s opportunism and the Western powers’ long sequence of failures (Manchuria, Abyssinia, Rhineland, Anschluss, Munich, Moscow 1939) shaped the conditions in which the trigger could be pulled. The verdict is therefore one of overwhelming but not exclusive responsibility.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the path to war from the failure of the Anglo-French-Soviet talks in summer 1939 to the British and French declarations of war on 3 September.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives. Developing: Events listed; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage. Indicative content: • April-August 1939: Anglo-French-Soviet talks dragged; Britain sent a junior delegation by slow ship; Poland refused Red Army transit. • Mid-August 1939: talks broke down; Stalin concluded the West was not serious. • 23 August 1939: Ribbentrop and Molotov signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact in Moscow; secret protocol divided eastern Europe. • 25 August 1939: Britain formalised its alliance with Poland; Hitler postponed the invasion briefly. • 1 September 1939: Germany invaded Poland at 4:45 a.m.; Wehrmacht used Blitzkrieg tactics. • 1-2 September 1939: Britain and France issued ultimatums demanding immediate withdrawal. • 3 September 1939: ultimatums expired; Britain (11 a.m.) and France (5 p.m.) declared war on Germany. • 17 September 1939: Soviet forces entered eastern Poland in line with the secret protocol; Poland ceased to exist by the end of the month.

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways in which the Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 was useful to Hitler.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points with relevant detail.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Securing the eastern flank: the pact removed the risk of a two-front war when Germany invaded Poland; without it, Hitler would have faced a possible Anglo-French-Soviet alliance, exactly the situation that crippled imperial Germany in 1914-18.
• Dividing Poland in advance: the secret protocol ensured Soviet entry from the east on 17 September 1939, so German forces did not need to occupy the whole country.
• Diplomatic shock: the pact stunned Britain, France and Japan; Tokyo distrusted Berlin afterwards, weakening the Anti-Comintern Pact.
• Limitation: the pact was always tactical — Hitler intended to break it, and did so when Germany invaded the USSR in June 1941.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the role of Hitler in the outbreak of war was different from the role of Stalin.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct ways clearly explained with precise context.
Secure: Two clear ways with relevant detail.
Developing: One way developed; second weak.
Emerging: General comment.

Indicative content:
• Active aggression: Hitler ordered the 1 September 1939 invasion of Poland; Stalin did not order any invasion until 17 September, after Polish military collapse, in line with a previously agreed secret protocol.
• Long-term aims: Hitler had pursued territorial revision and Lebensraum since 1933 across a sequence of crises; Stalin’s eastward moves were short-term opportunist gains made possible by the Pact.
• Diplomatic position: Hitler positioned Germany as the prime mover throughout the 1930s; Stalin reacted to the failure of Western alliance talks and chose the better of the two offers on the table.
• Public role: Hitler made the speeches and the demands; Stalin signed the Pact only after the Anglo-French talks had collapsed.

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways in which a 1961 academic article by A.J.P. Taylor (Source D above) is useful to a historian studying the outbreak of war in 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, supported by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points using content and either provenance or own knowledge.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: presents the structuralist case — Hitler as an opportunist exploiting circumstances rather than a master planner.
• Provenance: a major academic re-evaluation by a leading British historian, written with archival access and the benefit of distance from wartime emotion.
• Own knowledge: Taylor’s 1961 thesis was controversial at the time and remains so; it forced historians to engage seriously with the role of Western failure and the contingent nature of the path to war.
• Limitation: Taylor’s argument is a case to be tested, not a settled finding; modern historians (Kershaw, Evans) treat Hitler as both planner and opportunist, drawing on both intentionalist and structuralist traditions.
